Captain Selwyn, who will retire from the repre- sentation of the Wisbeach division, came down to the house yesterday, emptied his locker, and de- clared that that was the last Parliament would see of him.

In the course of the Aquarium slander case, Mr. Lockwood requested that the marionette dols might he accommodated with seats in the court whereupon Mr. Justice Hawkins observed that, if he acted according to precedent, perhaps they ought to be accommodated with seats on the bench.

The Select Committe on the Childien's Life Insur- ance Bill, which has practically suspended its inquiries in consequence of the death of Dr. Ragee, will, I hear, hold a further meeting under the chairmanship of Lord Derby. It is unlikely, how- ever, that any further evidence will be taken this session, and the bill will have to take its chance an- other year.

Emperor William is bringing over with him to England his brother-in-law, the Duke of Augusten- burg, the nephew of Prince Christian, for whom his Majesty wishes to arrange a marriage with one of the daughters of the Prince of Wales, for whom the Duke would be a misergble match. He is exceed- ingly proud and arrogant, desperately stupid, and by no means rich.

The large number of ladies on the terrace of the Houses of Parliament on Saturday, and the jun- ketting with strawberries and cream and afternoon tea that was going on suggested an inquiry as to Whether a garden party was being held. Parties are not allowed in Parliament ; individdal members may bring in two or three ladies apiece, and may " accidentally " assort themselves into parties on the terrace, but .anything in the shape of an organ- ised party is strictly forbidden.

Sir William Gordon Cumming purchased his lieu- tenancy and captaincy in the Scotch Guards. The money-value of these commissions and the recog- nised over-regulation price he forfeits on his removal from the Army. When Major Walter Har- bord was removed from the Army some years ago for a similar offence,he lost the regulation and over- regulation value of a majorship in the 7th Hussars. Colonel Valentine Baker lost the regulation value of a lieut.-colonelcy. lie had retired upon-half from the 10th Hussars, and had therefore received his" ever-regulation."

MANY great men have expressed a wish as to the kind of death they wanted to die, and they have mostly desired a sudden death. Perhaps, in this matter, old Fuller, who had thought over all possible modes of exit, arrived at the wisest con- clusion "None please me." FREDDY had been repeatedly told he must not ask people for money. One day he met an old gentleman who could never resist an appeal from the small boy. "Mr. X.," said Freddy, "do you ever give threepenny-bits to little boys that don't .aalt for 'em ?" He got the money. A LADY promised to give her maid £5 as a mar- riage portion. The girl got married to a man of low stature, and her mistress on seeing him was .surprised, and said—" Well, Mary, what a little ,husband you have got !" "La !" exclaimed the ,girl, "What could you expect for £5 ?" A LacTunza wished to explain to a little girl how a lobster casts its shell when he has outgrown it, so, by way of illustration, he said—" What do you do when you have outgrown your clothes? You throw them aside, don't you ?" "Oh no," ,said the little one, "we let out the tucks." -6' Mu SISTER (shouting to Bobby)—" Bah-bee! 'You are wanted to do an errand." "Why—why (after a long pause) such a leg .as you'd clean a flute with !" A MAN was at the circus watching a family of acrobats performing a feat termed the huthan ladder. I like young fellows who are capablb of supporting a family." " The old gentleman had to cough, look learned, and go away when his youngest answered, more logically than his parent, "If I eat it, how can I have it when I want it? A YOUNG man, recently married, suggested to :his wife that they should argue some question frankly and fully every morning in order to learn more of each other. The first question happened to be "whether a woman could be expected to get along without a hat," and he took the affirmative; and when last seen he had climbed into a hayloft and was pulling the ladder after him. No," said the young man at the box office, "I don't want an end seat; I want one in the middle of the row. I usually go out two or three times during the performance, and always between the acts, and half the pleasure I get at the theatre is the sensation I make in passing in and out, you know. No, no; no end seat for me. A fellow ;light go out and come in a dozen times and nobody would notice him." ".Well,' responded an elderly lady, "I've read somewhere that conscience makes cowards of us all.' And as • lawyers mostly have no consience, why of course they haven't anything to make them cowards." "How is your husband this afternoon, Mrs. Skeggs ? A most outrageous job has been quietly perpe- trated at the War Office for the benefit of Lord Wolseley, who has so long pulled the strings at that hot-bed of favouritism and nepotism. The Irish command has always been a Lieutenant-General's berth, with emoluments amounting to £2,558 a year. It has now been made the command of a full General, the result being that Lord Wolseley will in future receive £3,588 a year. This has been done without a shadow of justification, and Parliament has not been consulted in any way whatever. There never was a worse job, even-in the scandalous times when the Duke of York ruled at the Horse Guards.;

A curious Custon House dispute is reported from Duisburg, in Germany. A high legal official there is an ardent cryllector of butterflies, and sent lately to Holland for specimens. The butterflies arrived safely at Duisburg, but were detained at the Cus- tom House. An inquiry elicited the fact that the Customs officials had come to the conclusion that as butterflies had wings they must be classed as poultry! and so be subject to the same duty. It was only after some time and patience had been expended on the part of the entomologist that the authorities finally concluded that butterflies came within the domain of scieuce and art, and were not subject to duty.

The Lycian tombs which have hitherto been seen in the entrance hall of the British Museum, are about to be transferred to the new mausoleum- room. These marbles it will be remembered, were brought over from Lycia, in Asia Minor, by her Majesty's Government in the years 180-6, under the direction of Sir Charles Fellows.. In the place of these tombs a representative series of Greek and Latin inscriptions will be exhibited. Among the most interesting of the Greek inscrip- tions there will be one about 560 8.C., record- ing the dedication of some work of art by the sons ot Anaximander, and the name of the artist, Terpsicles.

Bishop Temple used to be known as the bishop of the liberals. He still seems to have some of his ancient progressiveness lurking in his nature. In Convocation he had to bring up for the considera- tion of his brothers of the bench some resolutions on education passed by the Chamber which repre- sents the "inferior clergy." Among them was an absolute caveat against free education. His lord- ship of London not only struck it out, but shocked the Bishop of Ely and some other bishops by frankly advising the managers of Church schools to bring the parents into joint control with themselves by making the representatives of the fathers sharers in their consultation. Thi.) was a form of outside control 'which had been tried and found to work.

Ms'v Mr. and Mrs. Parnell be happy! But would suggest to them whether it might not be well for them seriously to consider if this happiness is not more likely to be attained by indulging in the bliss of privacy than by endeavouring to prolong a hopeless struggle, which has already done great harm to the cause and the country whose welfare Mr. Parnell professes to have at heart. Mr. Farnell loses no opportunity ot stating hew much he owes to his Egeria, but it is hardly likely that the Irish will (with all respect to the lady) accept her as their uncrowned Queen, and allow her to rule under the nominal headship of her husband. Antony may , have been right or wrong in giving up the world for Cleopatra, but he, had the sense to see that he gave it up when he followed Cleopatra in her flight.

"Dog shows," in the opinion of " Ouida," have become "a pest." No man who really cares for dogs-1 would, she considers, submit them to the torment of imprisonment at these competitive gatherings for the sake of medals and prizes. More- over, this lady scorns the notion that by this means the breeds ate improved. The dog-judges, she observes, are all of them dog-sellers, and set up a wholly arbittary and often most foolish standard of excellence, setting down in true Justice Shallow fashion mere fantastical rules as to what is or is not good form in their sapient sight. As an example, the fact is cited that the English judges decide that the hair of a Maltese dog should be straight, whereas the Maltese dog in his full beauty should have a wavy and even a curly coat, his fine, soft hair falling in long ringlets, like a child's long hair. " Ouida " accounts for this by the suggestion that one of these dog-judges, who evidently knew nothing about the original breed, invented this un- usual condition because it suited some exhibitor at some time or other.

Mr. Balfour hoped to see similar schemes established for the benefit of all classes,and especi- ally in the rural districts. But he did ,not believe it possible that other societies could give so large a rate of interest as 4 per cent. Mr. Chamberlain pro- poses by State aid to give 5 per cent.

The Queen was not favoured with the, usual Queen's weather on her visit to town on Monday to witness the Royal christening, and the heavens wept profusely over the ceremony of giving a name to the little Royal lady. Her Majesty was in her ele- ment. Nothing delights her domestic soul more than such little domestic ceremonies, and her simple happiness on such occasions it is good to see. The Queen needs these little innocent excitements just new to wipe out the painful memory of the recent card scandal, which I am told by an authority, grieved the Queen more than anything has done since the death of Prince Consort, except the loss of her two children Princess Alice and Prince Leopold. The filial devotion of Princess Beatrice to her Royal mother is very pretty. At the Ponsouby wedding the other day a lady whose windows overlooked the entrance to the chapel noticed how before the Queen entered Princess Beatrice arranged her Majesty's bonnet and disentangled her parasol from the white lace bonnet strings. Now that the Queen is becoming'quite an old lady (we are apt to forget how old she is) the constant care and companion- ship of such a daughter must be the greatest com- fort to her, and all honour is due to the Princess, who has been so faithful tea trust which doubtless must sometimes entail considerable self-sacrifice and monotony.

Amongst other people whO have been deeply struck with Mr. Chamberlain's proposals for old- age pensions is Mr. Balfour; but he is not yet per- suaded as to the practicability of the scheme. The Chief Secretary was the prize.speaker at a meeting on Monday night of the depositors of the savings bank associated with the South-eastern and Metro- politan Railway Companies. The savings bank is entirely controlled by the employes, but the com- panies pay 4 per cent. on their investments—ft rate ; of 1 per cent. higher than they can borrow in the open market. "The question," said Mr. Balfour, "is whether it is an advantage given to the em- ployes which carries with it any evil consequences. En my opinion it does not. THERE are plenty of people who mix their religion with their business, but who don't stir it up well. The business invariably rises to the top. TIME is always represented earring a scythe, and we suppose he will continue to carry this primitive agricultural weapon until time shall be no mower. _ _

.. --- SAM JONES says—" Live so your children may put their feet in your tracks and be honourable. That is don't walk all over road on the way home at nights. A WITTY lady remarked of a gentleman noted for his taciturnity and arrogance, "He seems to me an anomaly in natural philosophy; he is gravity with- out attraction." HAPPINESS IS defined by Madame de Stael to be "a state of constant occupation upon some desirable object, with a continual sense of progress towards its attainment."
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 4, 1891.

div.head: ACROSS TAR ATLA.I'TEIC (No. 4.)
div.p: ACROSS TAR ATLA.I'TEIC (No. 4.)
BY "TOWNSMAN." ON THE CARS.
AMERICAN TICKETS-BAGGAGE CHECKING-THE
NEWSBOY-THE RAILWAYS-THE BRIDGES-THE
ENGINE'S BELL.

"All aboard "cries the conductor, "clang, clang; slang, clang " rings the engine bell, and the train starts on its thousand mile trio to Chicago. We are in for 36 hours' steady running,so I settle down to a series of novel sensations, sensations such as can only be experienced in a new world. The train con- sists of a powerful locomotive of native design, a baggage car,a smoking car,a day car, and a drawing room car, all of course on the Pullman principle, so that one can walk through the entire length of the train. The first novelty is the American, Railway Ticket.

div.head: TICKETS, TICKETS.
div.p: TICKETS, TICKETS.

As you buy a railroad ticket for the first time,you I pick up the novelty with considerable interest and I curiosity. You find it made of thin pasteboard about two inches wide, and as long almost,.in com- parison, as the journey you are about to make. The first six inches of the ticket are occupied with rules, regulations, and instructions, and along two sides of these are the dates and names of the months. and the years of the next decade. The rest of the ticket consists of ]in. by 21n. sections, from point to point, as a rule, for every 200 or 300 miles of the journey. There are three kinds of tickets. The first is the first-class, which is charged so 'much a mile, and is available fog any length of time, and for journeying from one city to another at your leisure. % The second is the second-class, which is described as a limited ticket, that is, you have so many days only allowed in which to complete your journey. Then, there is the limited express ticket, for a fast train, for which you have to pay almost double fare: If you buy an unlimited ticket for a long journey, and circumstances arise by which you determine not to pursue it, you just walk into a ticket agency in the city in which you find your- self,and sell the unused portion of the ticket for the highest sum you can get. As this proceeding is of very frequent occurrence, a large business is done in these transferred tickets, and in every-large city a host of agencies exist, many of which make a feature of advertising "cut rates." If you probe the matter, however, you find there is very little "cutting" done,. as the agency invariably demands nearly the full fare. Directly the train has started, the conductor comes along to examine and collect the tickets. If you are going through- with the train, the collector punches yopr ticket,..and then gives you a bit of blank pasteboard, coloured ac- cording to distance, and white if you're booked through. This you wear in your hat, and it saves you from having to show your passport every time the train starts and new corners board it. About every 200 and 300,miles you have to show the ori- ginal ticket, and a portion is detached, so that your ticket shortens with the journey, Until eventually you have none left. The dates are not stamped on the ticket as in England, but holes are punched in the figures previously mentioned as being printed along the side, and as you journey on punch after punch is put through your ticket until you begin to fear there will be nothing to punch- by-and-by. The conductors are mostly elderly meals,. and after discharging their duties, they come an sit by and chat with their friends or acquaintances on the train when it is doing a long run. But befo,re boarding the cars, you have an experience with the

div.head: BAGGAGE-CHECKING SYSTEM.
div.p: BAGGAGE-CHECKING SYSTEM.

You walk into the baggage room at the depot, as the station is called here, hand in your, baggage, and receive in exchange a brass check, which you pre- sent at the end of your journey, and receive for it your possessions. Once having checked your lug- gage you need have no further anxiety regarding it as you will find it all right when and where you want it. The system ia.of inestimable benetlt on the long journeys which the Americans-have to make, and it is to be hoped English Railway CAI'S will adopt the system in its entirety before long. The train was well filled with passengers, but.the trt*prity ot them left the cars before sunset. Hardly,. has the train started when

THE. NEWS33OI.I- comes round with the Boston papers, When he has supplied the demand for these he re-appears with his arms filled with shilling novelsi.arie of which he, drops by every passenger in the. cars. The pas- sengers pick them up, look at the.titles, and then lay the books down. The boy on his return retakes. possession of his wares at thozametime endeavour- ing to push trade by suggesting raor6 attractive titles. But it is no use :- the travellers are not. in a reading mood. The persistent trader, how- ever, again appears, this. time with the month/ye- magazines, and the New York comic weeklies, andi distributes them as coolly as if he had idst arrived:. Business, however, is dreadfully slack, and he • slowly picksup his treasures and disappears. stia,. it is only for a few minutes, at the end of which time he comes along with a. basket of candy. and fruits, and this time manages to tempt the juvenile portion of the passengers into spending a few cents. This performance is repeated after everystoppage, and is renewed so very oftenelnrieg the day that the presence of the boy becomes almost un- bearable, and at last you refuse to look at him, or hia wares. "This boy," remarked a doctor traversing the continent, "is a positive nuisance, and I wonder he is tolerated. I never patronise him except for a paper." I soon discovered that that was all the patronage the bulk ot passengers bestowed upon him. THE CONDITION OV THE RAILWAYS. The American railways, orraiiroads as they are oalied, are all laid on the level, and the gradient rises and falls only according to the configuration of the country through which they pass. As a general rule they Nlow the course of livers, and it is no uncommon thing for a river to have arailroad running on either side and a line of steamers on the surface of it. The track, as the American permanent way is called, bears no .consparison to the stability and hnish of an Enelishaine. No rail- way chairs are used to secure the rails to the. sleepers, the rails being simply nailed direct to the Okeper, the latter itself being invariably rotten. I frequently took a walk down the track, and as I stepped from tie to tie (i.e sleeper) the rotten wood gave way under me, and I was constantly slipping along. No doubt therotten state of the sleepers is due to the intensity of the climate, but at the time of my visit no attempt Wait made to renew, them, and they gave one the impression that such a. state of the line was a usual thing. The rails, too, aro very unevenly laid, but • for all that the Pullman cam glide fairly smoothly along there.,, though at times cars. have such a serious" list" on them, you wonder where you are going. The track, hew.ever, gives little cause for anxiety. It is when you come tothe railroad bridges that you begin to quake. Many of these structures cross broad and swiftly flouring rivers, and they are of the most flimsy-looking description, considering the strain they have to bear. As a rule they celery only single lines, and this seems more than they can do with safety. The majority of the bridges are tressit built,but in some few cases iron-work has been substituted. Even where this is the case the girders are so fsagile-looking that you fancy the builders have been trying how close they can get to the metaphorical "'last straw," and the feeling of passengers unaccustomed to such delicate, structures is not over pleasant. This uncomfortable feeling is intensified as you discover that on approaching I, a bridge the driver of the train will slow oft almost to a.: Jead slow, and will then drive his engine as cautiously as if he every minute expected the bridge to open before leim. and 'precipitate the train into the depths below, So

cautious indeed are the drivers that more than once our train came to a standstill right in the middle of bridges, and some of the passengers thought this was done to give them time to appreciate the scenery !

div.head: AMERICAN STATIONS.
div.p: AMERICAN STATIONS.

American depOts, or railway stations, are also on a par with the tracks. It is only in the great cities that the railroad companies erect stations at all equal to those on English railways, and these for originality of design surpass anything in the "Little Island." But the depots at wayside stations are the meanest erections you ever put eyes on. Cities of 40,000 inhabitants can only boast of a wooden barn-like structure that serves as booking office, waiting room, and baggage office. There is no platform as in England. The train pulls up opposite the depot, and the passengers on alighting have to walk across the metals to the waiting room, or the way out. Frequently, on a long journey, the train will pull up at a solitary station pitched in the middle of a field, close by the spot where a narrow road, more nearly resembling a trail than anything, is crossed by the line. Hardly a house is to be seen, and the only signs of life are two or three buggy teams that have been driven in to meet the train. Even in a big city a singular feature of an Amer- ican dippoo," as an Irish-American pronounced the word, is the death-like stillness that pervades the place when the trains are out. Only three persons can usually be found about the station. They include the station- master, who does the booking, the telegraph operator, and the baggage clerk. At certain depots, where there is a refreshment bar, there are also a bar tenter and a waiter or two. Porters are unknown in a country where they have a strong belief in helping themselves, and they are, as a matter of fact, rendered unnecessary by the excellent baggage checking system in vogue. The roads are entirely unprotected', and it is startling to a new corner to see the rails laid along the main street of a city, without the slightest attempt to protect the public from being run down. Whenever the rails inter- sect a road a light signboard in the shape of a cross is erected bearing the legend—" Railroad Crossing. Look out for the cars !" but in the night it is impossible to see'these notices, and as a consequence the loss of life on the railways is simply frightful. In a city of over a hundred thousand inhabitants the train ran for miles alongside the footpath, and one could have touched the houses through the car windows with apparently very little trouble.. The only warning the people get of an approaching train is the ringing of

div.head: ENGINE'S- BELL.
div.p: THE ENGINE'S- BELL.

The bell rings at every level crossing, it rings when anything is on the track, it rings on entering a city, rings whilst in it, and rings when leaving it. It seems to unaccustomed ears as if the bell never ceased ringing, and the " clang, clang ; clang, clang,"bf the deep-toned monster so impresses itself upon your nervous system that it complete iy takes possession of you. In lying down and in rising up you fancy you'llear the sound of alarm ; you wake in your sleep with it ringing in your ears, and you start when walking on the streets as you imagine the dreaded thing is behind you. It takes days to get rid of the melancholy warning voice, and still longer to regain possession of your confidence. Even as I write, the ominous sound floats across he air,and tells me a train is rapidly .approaching the city depot. (Tole concluded next 'week).
COCK-FIGHTING IN THE BLACK COUNTRY.

The crusade against cock-fighting in,the "Black I Country" goes briskly on. At tha• Sourbridge Police Court a large batch of cock-fighters have just been convicted and fined in various amounts, and from the evidence there can be no doubt that this cruel sport is still widely practised in surreptiti- ous way in the districts of Cradley and Wolver- hampton. All the usual, apparatus of the old cockpits—as steel spurs, scales, welghts, water- bottles, and sponges, were found upon some of the accused. They had als• in their possession carrier pigeons. supposed to be wanted to carry the news to distant places for the satisfaction of: those who had "put money," as Lord Salisbury says, on the event. While cock-fighting is pursued in this systematic fashion, it is impossible not: to suspect that evidence of the fact might-with alittle energy have been collected before.. It is satisfactory, how- ever, to note that the police are now doing their duty. The cruelty of the proceedings of these " sportsmen 7 was abundantly • proved.,. That some of them are persons of means may be inferred from the fact that they arrived in a four-hone. drag. It is stated that one of the cocks, "-scientifically I trimmed and in fine fighting form,' was produced in court, and "crowed repeatedly." Seeing that his I share in the business was certainly less disgraceful than that of his masters, his: right to, crow seems unquestionable.

div.head: QUEER AT A CHRISTENING,
div.p: THE QUEER AT A CHRISTENING,

The Queen, with, Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg, left Windsor nt eleven o'clock on :limbs' morning to attends the christening of the daughter of the Duke and Duchess of -Fife 'which took place, at noon at the Chapel Royal, St. Janaes"s„, the names given to the Infant being Alexandra )(intone, Alberta Edwina Louise. The Queen acted as chief spooser. the other godmothers and godfathe being the Queen of Denmark,,the infant's great grandmother, the. Princess Victoria of Wales, the Prince of Wales, and the Duke of Clarence. The cere- mony was performe'l by the Archbishop of Canterbury, assisted by the Bishop of London and other clergymen. The water used was brought from the River Jordan by Lord llowton. At the conclusion of the ceremony. the Queen gave the infant a hearty kiss, and the child was caressi,d and much admired by all the members of the family. The Queen subsequently left for Paddington on ' her return to Windsor. •

GENIUS AND INSANITY.

Writiog about Mr; iisbet's new work on "The Insanitly of Genius,'" Professor Tlluxley thus ex- presses his views Genius to my mind moans innate capacity of any kind above the average mental level. From a biological point of viow, I sholald say that a genius among men stands in the same position as a 'sport' among anircials and ' plants, and is. a product of Oa variability which is the postulate of selection both natural tuad artifi- Qiel. On the general ground that a strong and therefore markedly abnormal variety is not likely to be so well in harmony with existing conditions as the normal standard (which has been brought to what it is largely by the operation of those condi- tions),l should say that a large proportion of genius sports' are likely to come to grief physi- cally and socially, and that the intensity of ftsAing which is one of the conditions of what is called genius, is especially liable to run into the 4, fixed ideas' which are at the bottom of so much insanity."

A: mass meeting :to encourage the Millers was held on I,londay night. In accordance with a notice sent in to the master fustian cutteradnf blaceleafield and Congleton recently, asking ,for an advance iu prices, and the Inzsters not haykag acceded to their request, the operative cuttera,cf the above town& came out on strike on Saturday. THE EAXDOCK FIT SHAFT DisiaTEß.
FURTHER DETAILS.

The shocaing colliery -:accident at fitydoesk, on Thursday night week by which four men ,lnet 'their Jives and two others sustained serious injury, -caused A gloom and a general feeling of depression through- cut the wide area known as the Haydock coal- leld, including Haydocl, Earlestown, NaWtCn,k- Gnlborne, and Ashton -in - BialcerAeld. Air. Henry Hall, the Government inspector of mines for the district, visited the colliery on Friday at won,i and inspected the shaft of the ring Pit and the worldne arrangements. In accordance with their usual practice in accident cases, the firm of Wssrs. Evans and Coin-. pany provided gccd substantial coffins for the interment of the remains:

THE VICAR OF HAYDOC4 A.STD THE CALAMITY. The Rev. A. M. Lewis, M.A„ vicar of the parish, , preached in Haydoek Church on Sv.uday morning from the words, "The end is come, and I will judge thee ' according to thy ways "Ezekiel vii.2nd and 3rd verses). He stated that sad events had recently taken place amongst them—sad enough to make them think a little of the ead of all things. The whole parish had been startled out of its ordinary bearing by the awful visita- tion which had cut down instantly and without any warning four strong healthy lives. They entered on the work of their dangerous calling--one, he believed, des- cending the shaft for the first time,and 'in a few seconds all that could be told of their humanity was that four bodies had fallen and lay crushed and broken at the bot- tom of the dreadful shaft. Death was constantly at work, and in that parish where most men followed a dangerous calling they often saw the ambulance hurriedly driven in one direction or another, and their hearts were in their mouths lest its burden should ba some dear brother, hus- band, or son. He exhorted them to prepare for the day of death, and expressed a hope that even in that awful passage through the shaft some prayer for mercy issued from the lips of the men which would not remain un- answered. He asked them to use such a sad end as a means for the working out of their own salvation, and said that with all men a time would come when the sun should rise for the last time, and when men would work and take their food for the last time, The lesson for each and all was that their lives should be such that at the last God might be able to say, "Well done thou good and faithful servant." THE INQUEST

The inquest on the bodies of the four men who were killed at the King Pit, Haydock, near St Helens, belong- ing to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. ,on Thursday night. was formerly opened before Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, at the Waggon and Horses Hotel, Haydock, on Saturday forenoon. The names of the unfortunate men were Michael Cawlfield, 25 years of age of 32, Wood- st., Earlestown; Thomas Sharp, 39, of 7, Liverpool-rd., Ashton-in-Makerfield ; Patrick M'Hugh, 30, of 13, War- rington-road, Ashton-in-Makerfield ;. and Albert Marsh- all, 45, of 65, Tamworth-St., Earlestown. On Saturday morning the bodies had been placed in the coffins sup- plied by the firm, and were ranged on tables in the lecture hall connected with the collieries. Mr. John Pilling was foreman of the jury, and Mr. John Robinson, general manager, represented Messrs Evans and Co. The Deputy-Coroner' addressing the jurors, said that before commencing to take the evidence be wished to explain that two of the men in that unfortunate accident were suffering from the injuries they had received, and would not be able to attend to give evidence that day. It would be absolutely necessary for them to adjourn, and consequently he intended only to take evidence of identi- fication, so as to enable him to give orders for burial. He suggested that they might then adjourn for a fortnight, because the doctor had said it would be a fortnight before the men would be able to attend.—Nancy Sharp, of 7, Liverpool-road, Ashton-in-Makerfield, was then called. She stated that the deceased, Thomas Sharp, was her hus- band, anEl had been employed as a brickstter. He was 39 years of age.—Mary M'Hugh, 51, Bedworth-st., Liver- pool, deposed' that the deceased Patrick M'Hugh was her brother, and was aged 30. He was a sinker, and had lived at 13, Warrington-road. Ashton-in-Ma kerfield.—Eliza Marshall, 65, Tamworth-st., Earlestown, said the de- ceased Albert Marshall was her husband, and he was 45 years of age.—Thomas Cawlfield, 29, Adelaide-st., Wigan, gave evidence that he was a brother of the deceased Michael Cawlfield.
The jury then consulted, and it was arranged that the inquest should stand adjourned until Monday, the 13th July.

This will form a lazge sheet of water which, after dredg- ing, will be available for vessels of any size. A lock is quite complete which will connect this dock with the Weaver Navigation (which is built parallel with the river), and through the lock will come the large and im- portant traffic from the salt districts of Cheshire. The lock is of very considerable dimensions. being 229 ft. long and 42ft. wide; other locks are being constructed a short distance above the Weaver to admit boats to and from the docks at Weston Point and Runcorn. This work, however, will not be finished for some months to come. It is the length from the mouth of the Weaver to Eastham with which the makers of the canal have been most concerned hitherto, for it was directed by Parliament that this section should be opened before certain pointts nearer Warrington could be touched.

div.head: SNIP 'CANAL.
div.p: THE SNIP 'CANAL.
PROWESS OF THE WORKS ON THE EASTHAM
SECTION.

Since the flooding of thelength of the Manchester Ship Canal between Eastham and Ellesmere Port some dis- quieting statements have been made with regard to slips and breads in theembankment. Liverpool contem- Meary on Tuesday even suggested that a great portion of the embankment will have to be" reconstructed in a rsuchmore solid form." It may be well to say that there is not the least reason for alarm. Some mishaps, as.wasinevitalle, have occurred, but all the injury that has beec done a very few days' work will put right. TheEastham cutting was in pro.ress for four years, and duringthat time was free fromefloods. It would have been remarkable if, when the ,water was at length ad- .mitted, there had been no such sliding of the banks as has occurred. But to speak of reconstruction in the 'large style quoted above is not unlike suggesting that a new mansion should be rebuilt'because a small portion 1 Of 'freshly placed stucco work had fallen. What has oeuurred was expected to occur, and possibilities much more serious had to be faced when the water was let in. Them were indeed engineers who thought that the banks niigbt implaces be torn up by the sudden flood. There are altogether seventy miles of' Canal banks. For the most part they 'run through solid earth, in which of course no43reach can occur. Where embankments have been necessary the Canal Company have gone to consid- eralle expensem providing a superior kind of masonry, not a stone of which has given way. Now that the Eastham part of the canal is full, the motive power that .basreaused the slight disturbances of which so much has been made is no longer at work.
OLLESMERE PORT "WiIiFFIC.

\ 'Within a very few days the traffic of the Shropshire 'Fajen Canal from Ellesmere Port will ,pass down the Ship Canal and enter the Mersey through the Eastham gates. A hundred yards below the Port the flooded por- tionef the ShiWCanal is dammed alp. At the point where the dam is made there is a breach. in the estuary line of the canal wall. The opening is net wide, but it allows the tide to come up to the Port, add is the present exit and entrance for barge traffic. When in the course of a few days all is ready for the operation the breach will beamed and the dam removed, and the only tide which :Ellesmere will know is the tide whioll will come up the Ship Canal. Within five or six weeks after this portion of the work is accomplished, a stage even more interest- ing-will haveobeen reached. This will be the opening of a further length of about nine miles, .stretching from ;Ellesmere Port to the mouth of the Weaver. The great salt trade of Wintrord and Northwieh will then be carried by way of the canal, with the merchandise ,which comes ,from'Aridland navigations to Northwhich, where the re- markable " Anderton lift" is a connecting link. There are alew points,between Ellesmere Pert and the Weaver at which work has yet to be done. 7r•he river Gowy, a tributary of theXersey, has been one-cause of trouble. The Canal Company were not allowed to impound the •waters of this stream, and the .result was that they hadAto carry them fifty feet below the surface of ,tke.earth, or a depth of 16ft. below • the bed of the •canal. tunnel was built under the new waterway,on. the estuary sideof virich the surface was again,' found. Two syphons. each 0f.12ft., now carry the Gowy on its underground waX to the river. This has been a work of great difficulty, and • has delayed canal operations at this pcint. On the excavation of the old bed of the Govvy men and machines are hard at w >rk, and unless some unexpected hindrance occurs the trench will be veryquickly,completed. At the old lighthouse begin the Ince rocksceLtending fe7 about a mile. These presented a •very solid buttress for the canal makers to encounter. For lour years the wemen have been blasting the barrier away, and to-day it is as clean eut,as sawn tim- ber, it the top of the cutting we look from a height of riot less than 7Cgt. over an absolutely perpendicular Cliff. 'The section 'extends three and a half miles further, to

div.head: IFIE MOITMCF TEE WELTER.
div.p: IFIE MOITMCF TEE WELTER.

Thispart of the eanal is completely finished, and for four months the surface water has been allowed to ac- cumulate in it, till there is ncw a uniform depth of five feet. Thisfinishedportion looks extremely well,,for there is no wide estuary with which to compare it. 'For the most part the straight line of banks is made of pitching, of a eandstone redness, but in places the surface is agree- ably broken by faseine work. This style of embanktnett is not uncommon on the canal,,,r.nd though it is not per- haps quite so strong.a protection as the rock, it is cer- tainly more picturesque. The branches of the osier and , the willow are thickly laced and laid in line on the banks. into which they send roots and mare firm the soil. 'Very quickly they send forth shoots, and in places where the planting is not quite recent the banksare now pleasantly green. The cmial wallis carried on through the estuary, and in front of the mouth of the 'Weaver. Within the next few weeks that river will discharge itself no longer into the Mersey but intothe canal, The canal people 4 however, are by Act of Parliament prevented from rob- bing the Mersey of this quantity of water, and the pro- blem of the engineer was how to meet this condition. This has been done by the ettection of the largest sluices which the world has yet known. They are 10 in number, each 30ft. wide, and the machinery is so perfect that a young bay could control it. The sluices are used not merely to regulate the passage of the Weaver water out .of the mud, but to admit the tidal flow. With their solid masonry and vast roller frames they present a very imposing piece of en- gineering work. Side by side with the sluices it a weir in the embankment, 600 ft. long, at a level of Nft. 2in., which is the mean level of high water and the height at Which the water opensthe lock gates at Eastharn. The ' embankment of the Weaver pens the water upthat river •to Frodsham, a distance of three miles from the canal.

div.head: LwritiVG IN THE TIDE AT EASTHAM.
div.p: LwritiVG IN THE TIDE AT EASTHAM.

The work at the mouth of the Manchester Ship Canal is now so far completed that on the morning tide of Thursday water was admitted direct from the Mersey to the sluices and locks at Eastham. It may be explained that a dam, partly natural and partly artificial, has been left by the engineers immediately outside the lock gates at Eastham, and which, rising some distance above high- water mark, prevented any inflow of water until the completion of the section. While the process of filling the completed first section by the temporary weir constructed at Ellesmere Port was in progress the dam at Eastham remained unmolested, but as soon as the water bad at- tained the necessary height, and the banks of the canal had proved their stability and freedom from any serious flaws, the energies of the executive staff were directed to the task of removing this dam. A large number of workmen, therefore, have lately been engaged in this particular piece of work, and the surface of the dam during the last few days has disappeared with marvel- lous rapidity. On Wednesday operations were suffi- ciently advanced to allow of two small sluices being cut through that portion of the dam opposite the entrance of the middle lock, preparatory to cutting the whole width of the passage. The two sluices were finished at low water on Wednesday evening, and on Thursday morning, as the tide gradually rose, the inflow of water from the Mersey direct into the canal took place. The shutters of the temporary weir at ,Ellesmere Port were also opened, and the water in the canal reached on Thursday the maximum depth of 26 feet. When the tide receded a considerable amount of water was allowed to flow through the sluices back from the canal into the river. The principal, in fact practically the only, obstacle which now prevents the commencement of traffic on the completed section is the remaining portbn of the dam which divides the river bed from the lock gates ; and the work of cutting a passage through this, it,is anticipated, will beconcluded in a few days. As we have previously stated, the mid- dle lock of the three is the lock which will ba used for traffic until the completion of the whole scheme, and the channel which leads to it from the river to the dam, beyond which are the lock gates, has already been cut and dredged to deep water. The work is being pushed on with all speed, large numbers of men being engaged day and night in the .completion of this part of the undertaking.

On Saturday last 352 members and employes of the Bolton Co-operative Society paid a visit to Runcorn to view the Ship Canal works in the locality. The large party was met at Widnes by Mr. T. Riles and Mr. T.. Watcon, two prominent members cf the :Runcorn Co- opemtive Society, who kindly acted as guides. Their railway tickets allowed them to cross the bridge without pa.snient of the usual toll of 2d., and then they proceeded alongsthe river-side and viewed the Ship Canal works in progrecs, and exhibited much intereelben what they saw. The doers at Runcorn and Weston Foist alsocame in for notice. Tea was provided at Forester's Halt; the visitors being well catered for by Mr. William Grounck, confec- tioner, Devonshire Square. A SHIP CANAL LABOURER DROW.NED AT LATCH-

div.head: FORD.
div.p: FORD.

Some children on their way from •school on Monday afternoon okserved a body floating lathe Old Quay Canal at Latchford. The attention of P.C. Wade, who hap- pened to be on duty near the scat, was called to the dis- covery, and that officer, with the assistance of John:Ross, a wsrkman in She employ of the Corporation, recovered the body, which was that of a labonrer, from the water, and conveyed it to the Black Bear to await identification and an inquest. Subsequently, the bi .ad 7 was identified:as that of William Holder,aged 28,a Ship Canalilabourer at.ho laad lodged in Knutsford-road. Holder was lact seen alive on Wednesday, the 54th June, and was supposed by his friends to have gone to work on anotbez section of thc, canal. It is believed that in making his way along the canal side, he accidentally fell into the water.—The inquiry into the circumstances attending the man's death took place at the Black Bear Inn, on Tuesday evening, before Mr. H. C. Yates, county coroner.—The first witness called was Mr. Holder, brother of the deceased, who said he saw his brother for the last time on Tuesday, 23rd June, when he 'Appeared to be Very merry.—Mrs. Holder, wife of the last witness, said that the deceased came to her house on Wednesday last and

asked for some money. He was under the influence of drink at the time. She gave him some money, and was under the impression that he was going back to work on the canal. She had never heard him say that he intended to destroy himself.—P.C. Wade said that on the 29th June some children came to him and said that a man was in the canal. He ran to the spot indicated, in the company of a man named John R6ss, with whose assistance he succeeded in pulling the body out. Deceased was conveyed to the Black Bear Inn, and the officer searched him, and found nothing but a knife and hand- kerchief in his possession. There was no sign of violence. —John Ross was next called, and bore out the statement of the officer.—A verdict of "Found drowned" was returned.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. _ _ _
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. _ _ _

At the Ship Canal Hospital, on Tuesday- afternoon, Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, held an inquiry on the body of Robert Halliday, carpenter, who died from injuries received at the Runcorn section, on the 19th June.— William Morgan, Stony-lane, Runcorn, said he was as- sisting the deceased on the day in question, to repair some wagons. There were three or four wagons on the road, which was known as a "dead" one, and con- nected the main road and the cutting. Witness went away on an errand, and left the man repairing a board inside the wagon. Witness saw a train of wagons came down the cutting whilst he was away. At one point the wagons had to do a " flying " shunt. Some of the wagons become unhooked and ran on the line on which deceased was working. The next thing he saw was the deceased running from the wagons. Witness saw he was hurt, but before he could get near the injured man was put on an engine and taken to the hospital.—Edward Jones, engine driver,said he was in charge of the engine St. George, which was drawing a full train of wagons out of the cutting from the navvy. Witness was not aware that anyone was in the wagons on the line before hem. A short distance from the point there is a slight incline, and here witness thought the jolting must have unhooked some of the wagons.— Thomas Rodgers, spragger, said he tested the last wagon. After the wagons ran loose the whistle was blown. Witness after- wards saw Halliday sitting on a block of wood. His • arm was crushed, and witness tied a handerchief round it. The deceased also complained of his shoulder. —Dr. Parker, surgeon at the Ship Canal Hospital, said he received the deceased on the 19th June. He was suffering from a lacerated arm and hand. There were also contusions on his back and side. Witness considered the case a serious one. The man,who was perfectly con- scious, was put to bed. An operation was perform 4 by Dr. Jones, after which the deceased gradually sank into unconsciousness, and died on the 27th June from the shock.—Ellen Halliday said the deceased was her hus- band, and was about 55 years of age. The last time she saw him before the accident was at Lime-st., Station, Liverpool,on the 15th June. When deceased didn't come home from Runcorn, she went to see the foreman, who told her of the accident. Witness saw her husband at the hospitals He seemed to be quite rational, and said he was putting a screw into the wagon when the run- away wagons knocked him down and ran over him.— John Kenworthy, foreman, said the repairs were done in a " cripple " road. The deceased had no right to work there, as it was against orders. There was a place pro- vided for repairing wagons, but the men had done the work in the,place in question. Deceased had always been steady, and he had had some reliance on him.—The Coroner having reviewed the evidence, the jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical opinion.

Of the [forty-five soldiers arrested at Folkestone on • Tuesday only fifteen are detained in custody. These will be tried by the commanding officer. It is stated that ,when the riot commenced the soldiers believed some of Iheir comrades were detained at the station.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO SUPERINTENDENT ROLLING WORTH.

Information reached Stockport, on Saturday, of a serious accident to Superintendent Hollingworth (for- merly of Runcorn),chief of the Stockport Division of the Cheshire police, and resident at the County Police Sta- tion, Hazel Grove. On Friday evening he was thrown from his trap, and so seriously injured,that no hope was entertained of his recovery. About 5 p.m. three men were passing along Dudley-lane, near Otterspool Bridge, close to Romily, when they found the superintendent lying unconscious by the side of the road. It was at once seen that a serious accident had occurred, and that Mr. Hollingworth was severely injured. The right side of his head was terribly crushed, his nose was smashed, and he bled very profusely. His features were almost unrecognisable. One of the men, however, knew the officer by his clothing, and as they knew that he waslin the habit of travelling that way in his trap, they looked about for traces of the vehicle. They found the horse and trap some distance away, and, returning to the in- jured man, placed him in the conveyance and took him at once to his home at Hazel Grove. Superintendent Hollingworth remained unconscious,and succumbed late on Sunday night. The occurrence was surrounded with mystery until Monday, when, as asserted, a girl while looking through the window of a public-house saw Mr. Hollingworth thrown out of his trap. The medical gentlemen are of opinion that the horse bolted, and the sudden jerk threw the superintendent on to the curb- stone. Deceased was 53 years of age, and had been a member of the force 26 years, having served at Broxton, Crewe, Runcorn, Knutsford, and for the last two years having been chief of the Stockport Division. He intended to retire at the end of July, and was negotiating for the purchase of a small farm in Cheshire. INQUEST. On Tuesday, Mr. F. Newton, coroner, held an inquiry at the Bull's Head Hotel. Hazel-grove, with respect to the death of Mr. Joseph Hollingsworth. Frederick Shaw, clerk, deposed that the deceased was in the habit of driving in a dogcart to visit the various sections of his division, his horse being a spirited nervous animal. Deceased had told him of being thrown out of his tray once when passing through Stockport. James Bromiley Greaves, butcher, Romiley, said he was driving dcwn Bunker's-hill, Romiley, on Friday evening, and the deceased passed him, driving slowly and apparently havirag command of his horse. The , accident took place immediately afterwards. Other witnesses spoke to the fact that the deceased was thrown or fell out of his dogcart. Mr. Thomas Moore, surgeon, stated that deceased never regained consciousness after the accident. There was a large contused wound over the right eye; the bones of the nose were broken; the right nostril was cut through, and there was evidence of fracture of the base of the skull. Verdict "Accidental death."
FUNERAL.

The funeral took place at Mellor church on Wednes- day amid demonstrations of respect and regret. Police officers from all parts of Cheshire were present. div.head: CHESHIRE FARMER'S BA.NKRITFTCY.
div.p: A CHESHIRE FARMER'S BA.NKRITFTCY.

At the Manchester City Police Court, on Wednes- day, before the Stipendiary (Mr. F. J. lieadlam), John Campkin, bankrupt, a farmer by occupation, formerly of Dutton Hall Farrar near Preston Brook, Cheshire, was charged in response to a summons with obtaining £l,OOO by false pretences, and also with making a false declaration. Mr. W. L. Hockin, who prosecuted on behalf of the Directors of Public Prosecutions, stated that in October, 1889, the defendant found himself pressed by Mr. Acton, solicitor, for the sum of £230 which the defendant col- lected in his capacity as overseer of the township, and which he had used for his own purposes. The defend- ant entered into negotiations with Mr. Marson, solicitor, Norfolk-st., Manchester, for a loan of £l,OOO from a Mr. ' Marshall, of Weaverham, Cheshire. Mr. Ma rson and Mr. Marshall went over to Dutton Hall Farm, and made an in- inpection of the produce and furniture, and being satisfied in this respect that there was sufficient security for the amount required, providing that the liabilities of the defendant were not above a certain sum, they asked him to make out a list of his liabili- ties. He made out a list, showing that his total liabilities amounted to £1,227, which included a sum of £526 he was owing to the executors of a Mr. Warbur- ton. He said he was anxious to pay off this liability, and that was the principal reason why he wanted to borrow £l,OOO. He made no mention whatever of £230 due to the township. Having obtained £l,OOO he gave a bill of sale on his house and produce to Marshall, and also made a statutory declaration to the effect that his liabilities were not more than £1,227. After receiving the £l,OOO he the next day paid off the £230 owing to the guardians, and discharged some other liabilities, but did not pay off the liability of £526. He then absconded. A petition was presented against him by a creditor, and he was adjudicated a bankrupt. Subsequently he re- turned and was arrested. An investigation of his affairss showed that the liabilities instead of being £1,200 amounted to £ 't,ooo, and on the day he made the statu- tory 'declaration he wrote a letter to Mr. Acton, in which hesaid that his assets would realise, he expected,23,soo, and his liabilities we're 23.000. If there was a ha lance in his favour he trusted that it would be paid over to his wife. For his own oart, he expressed the intention of going to America. Mr. Hockin called Mr. i‘larsion, solicitor. Norfolk-st., Manchester, who bore out his' statement. Witness said Mr. Marshall had had to prove' in the bankruptcy, and he had obtained a dividend of 6s. CI the pound. Mr. Forshaw, Warrington, who' represented the defen- dant asked witness whether Mr. Mi.ershalijcould not have got the whole of his money if he had* been sharp enough. Witness said they could not 'get posses Vou directly until ' the bill of sale had been signed, because, •0° far as they then knew, there had been no breach of anv clause of the bill of sale.
Mr. C. J. Dibb, official receiver in bankx ilPtcY. was called, and after his evidence had been takei..* the ease was adjourned until Monday on the application Qf Forshaw.

div.head: VYRNWY PIPE-LINE ACROSS T_CE MERSEY.
div.p: THE VYRNWY PIPE-LINE ACROSS T_CE MERSEY.

A representation has been sent to the Corpora- tion of Liverpool from the Rivers Committee of the Warrington Town Council, stating that the flanges of the temporary pipe across the Mersey at Fidler's Ferry are visible at low water, and that the pipe is not laid beneath the bed of the river as required by the Board of Trade. The representation adds that on the 15th inst. the anchor of a flat belonging to Mr. Abel, of Runcorn, caught on the pipe, &V in order to avoid damaging the pipe or his vessel, Mr. Abel remained fast until the next tide, thereby be- ing put to great delay and inconvenience. No re- ply to this communication has been received from the Liverpool Corporation.
THE ACCIDENT AT FIDLER'S FERRY. MR. DEACON'S REPORT.

At the meeting of the Water (Vyrnwy) Works Com- mittee, at Liverpool on Tuesday, under the chairman- ship of Alderman John Hughes, the following report was read by by Mr. Deacon with reference to the recent accident at the Fidler's Ferry aqueduct tunnel :—" The face of the shield stood on Saturday night, the 20th inst., at 121 ft. from the centre of the Lancashire shaft. On Monday, the 22nd, an accident occurred, which for- tunately only affected the pe.rmanent work by delaying its progress for one week. It appears that on Sunday, the 21st, a workman entered the tunnel, and on going out improperly closed the outer door of the lock opening towards the tunnel. The small leakage through the inner door of the lock, also opening towards the tunnel, was sufficient to put the lock under pressure, and on Mon- day morning it was found impossible to enter without letting out air. The indirect consequence of this was that at about five o'clock on Monday afternoon a dis- charge of water past the open sheld, carrying a small proportion of sand, occurred. By thik means the sand at the face of the tunnel was greatly disturbed, and its resistance to the passage of the air, under pressure from the face of the tunnel, was weakened. During the week the contractors obtained two forty-ton Large loads of clay, which were tipped in the river above the spot where the displacement had cccurred. I have very little doubt thatthis will create the desired resistance to the passage of air, and that before this report is presented the driving will have recommenced." After this report had been read a telegram addressed to the Town Clerk, was received, stating that the tunnel work was going on satisfactorily on Monday, and 1 ues- day. The circumstances which led to the disaster were fully discussed, and some severe comments were made by one member as to the great delay which had taken place. But the majority expressed satisfaction that the untoward damage had been repaired, and that there was now an immediate prospect of getting a temporary supply from Vyrnwy.
-The boring operations in the permanent tunnel are now progressing satisfactorily. The whole of the sand and sediment has been removed, and work is being car- led on as if nothing had happened.

At a quarterly meeting of the London Baptist Associa- tion on Wednesday, a resolution was adopted deploring the increase of gambling, and anticipating with grave concern the effect which recent revelations in connec- tion with the Prince of Wales must have on the morals of the whole community.
LITTLE OF THE GtiN ; NOTHING OF THE DOG

When Rip Van Winkle awoke from his nap in the Catskill Mountains in America, he found himself an old man. His dog was dead long ago, and nothing was left of his gun but the lock and barrel. And 'when he went back to the village of Falling Water, where he used to live, nobody recognized him. His wife, believing him dead, had married the innkeeper. Right enough too, for Rip had lain on the mountain side sound asleep, for twenty years.

A long snooze ; but it seems to me I'd rather be asleep half my life at a stretch than to stop awake and be miserable. Yet here is a woman who says," I can truth fully say that for eighteen years I was never free from pain for a single day."
Mercy ! Think of that. What a wretched way to live! Yet I suppose millions of folk crawl along through the world in that style. Not because they want to.
Heavens, No! But because they can't help it. This was her situation, and an army of other women (besides crowds of men) can sympathise with her.

She says: "For over twenty years I was weak and sickly. At first I had a bad taste in the mouth, poor appetite, and an uncomfortable feeling at my chest and sides, and often tried to obtain ease by holding my sides with my hands. After eating I had great pain; it was like a load at my chest, and I could not bear it until I vomited all my food up. I would be quite faint from the want of food but iras afraid to eat. At times I had bad attacks of spasms which nearly doubled me up, and I rambled up and down the house for hours together, for I could not even lie down. Of course I lost a deal of

sleep, and in a morning was so weak and faint I scarcely knew how to get out of bed and downstairs. For eighteen years I was never free front pain for a single day. "I saw doctor after doctor, and took a great quantity of medicine without finding any real relief. They would not say what was the cause of my ailment. I was fast wasting away, and did not think I could live much longer, when one day in 1831 my husband heard from Mr. Joseph Cooper, of Bourne, of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, which he said had cured him. If lam spared,' I said to my husband, I will try it.' 1 did so, and before I had taken the firit bottle I found relief, and after taking four bottles more I was quite well and strong.
"That is now ten years ago, and I have been in good health ever since, taking just an occasional dose of the

syrup. After my recovery the clergyman said to my husband, 'Your missus gets about very different to what she used to do,' and he told him that Mother Seigel's Syrup had wrought the cure. People tell me I look better than I did twenty years ago, and I feel so strong that I can now dig potatoes and do work with

anyone, notwithstanding I am 65 years of age. "My husband suffered terribly from rheumatism and flux, and has found wonderful benefit from the same medicine. He says he would have been in the church- yard long ago but for Mother Seigel's Syrup. For my- self I can say it saved my life, and I wish others to know what it has done for me and mine. (Signed). Mrs. ESTHER AYR, wife of William Ayr, of Thurlby, near Bourne, Lincolnshire."
In this brief and simple way Mrs. Ayr tells a story the full details of which would fill a book. What hopes and fears! what hours of keen sorrow and deep darkness

she must have experienced. Yes, indeed. None can even imagine it except those who belong to the great Sisterhood of Suffering. Where she mentions one symptom of her disease she actually could have named a dozen. For her malady—the fearfully common and fatal one, indigestion and dyspepsia—has as many signs and forms as the mind has fancies, or the heavens have clouds. From it, as from sin, come a thousand pangs and pains to torment and to crush helpless humanity. Seeing what her great discovery has accomplished in this and multitudes of like cases, how. good a friend to her kind was Mother S./Aryl ! Rip Van Winkle awoke .from his nap to find himself old; Mrs. Ayr awoke from her long night of ilium to find herself young again. Is not the , moral plain enough for all the suffering millions in Eng- land.

div.head: BOLTON KICKING CASE.
div.p: THE BOLTON KICKING CASE.

VERDICT OF MURDER BY THE CORONER'S JURY, The inquest on the body of Henry Clayton, Bolton,who died,as alleged, from kicks inflicted by Carter Michael ' M'Dermott, was held on Tuesday. The evidence showed that there was considerable animus on the part of M'Der- mott, and that be most brutally attacked Clayton when, as a result of his injuries he was unable to defend him- self. Medical evidence showed that the violence was the cause of death. A verdict of" Wilful murder " was returned by the coroner's jury.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
It will be seen from the details given in another column that Tuesday's meeting of the Warrington Town Council is likely to be a warm one. There is quite a host of burning questions to the fore.

The Corporation of St. Helens have decided -to convert the house in Victoria Park into a Museum and Picture Gallery. It will make a good beginning. A Picture Gallery in a park,or in park-like grounds, is a pleasant combination, as witness the f amous gallery at Dulwich.

It is stated,on what seems to be good authority, that the Parnellites are scheming with the Tories 'with a view to unseating Mr. T. P. O'Connor, in Liverpool, at the next election. "Can such things be and overcome as like a summer cloud ? " Does Mr. Parnell think he can repeat the tactics of 188,5? He may try, but he will not succeed.

The Emperor of Germany is about to pay a visit to England, and it is to be hoped he will be re- eeived—as he deserves to be—with enthusiasm. He is more than a King ; he is a man who is really in earnest in seeking to improve the la of his fellow- men. Bismarck as the man of Blood and Iron has been deposed, and thg Emperor William as the man of Flesh and Blood has taken his place.

Lord Bramwell pounced, on Tuesday, upon the Brine Compensation Bill in the House of Lords; but its backing was too strong for him. On Thurs- day, the Winsford Local Board decided to call a special meeting for the purpose of befittingly recognising the services of the Duke of West- minister, Mr. Brunner, M.P., and all who have been concerned in the passing of the Bill through Parliament. Thus "All's well that ends well."

According to the Chief Constable of Warrington, a woman's pocket is situated at the back of the dress—" the handiest place for pickpockets." Good for the pickpocket; but it isn't handy for. the other fellow. We appeal to the husband who has been despatched to the wardrobe for "that purse in the dress-pocket." Was it handy? Did he ever find "that purse ? " And did the hurried search not cause him to make hurried remarks?

At the hearing of a charge of drunkenness, at the Daresbury Sessions, on Tuesday, it transpired that the defendant, who was a publican of Little Leigh, had told the police that if he was drunk he was on his private premises. The plea would have been good if the defendant had been living in a privato house; but in that case the police would not have been present. As a publican, he has re- sponsibilities as well as privileges, and, the case being proved, he was fined by the magistrates.

The Rivers Committee of the Warrington Cor- poration can say—" I told you so" with regard to the temporary pipe line across the Mersey for supplying Liverpool with Vyrnwy water. It has not been laid low enough, and already one flat has lost a tide through it. Seeing that the difficulty Is being caused through the Corporation of Liver- pool declining to take the good advice which was tendered them, the least they can do is to grant compensation in each case without making a fuss over it.

One blot upon the Education Bill is being re- moved. The absurd clause is to be dropped which Would have insisted upon a fee for children under five, whilst giving free education to those above five. It is practically settled that the fee-grant to be allowed by the State shall apply to scholars between three and fifteen. This will be an en- couragement to parents to allow their children to attend school until they have passed in all the standards, and in a few "extras.'

It is not likely that the Factories Bill will be Materially altered in the House of Lords, judging from the circumstance that the second reading Was passed, on Monday, without a division. The House of Commons insisted the other week—even to the defeat of the Government—upon the half- time age being raised from ten to eleven; and the peers have accepted that decision. There is a little soreness amongst the parents of factory operatives at the change but it will soon wear off, and in a year or two they will be ready to acknowledge that the change is an improvement.

Ws stated that the Triple Alliance between Germany, Austria, and Italy has been renewed for six years ; and that it may be regarded as a league of peace. When the nations grow wiser, the Alliance will include every civilised Power; and soldiers will simply be so many International Police to deal with the disorderly, or those who break international law. It will be just as easy, when the time is ripe for it, as preserving national law. In that day, there will be fewer Emperors and Kings and other tremendous personages, and the people will be everywhere in power.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, John Noon, on being brought before the magis- trates for keeping a dog without a license, pleaded that he had a wife and five children. As this sin- gular plea surprised the Bench—for it was not stated that the dog was there to " mind " the children—the defendant wished to know if it was recognised as a luxury for a working-man to keep a dog." To this curious question. the Mayor gave a curious answer. He said: "It is a luxury for anyone to keep a dog if he does not want one." Really now! But "is that so ?" A luxury when notwanted P. A nuisance rather.

The Dean of Norwich has been showing himself Open-hearted and liberal-minded to an interviewer from the office of the "Pall Mall Gazette." Refer- !jug to:that phase of modern religion which is Known by the name of" Missions," the Dean said: This spirit has not yet, to any extent, affected our cathedral system. Evangelization is regarded a's an outrage upon its dignity ; where it has been tried, most. encouraging results have followed." "Outrage upon its dignity "; that is a good phrase, and how true! And what a contrast to the methods of the apostles! Try to fancy Paul hesi- tating about his dignity, when there were souls to be saved?

There seems little hope ipf the Rating of Machi- nery Bill becoming law this year; and meantime mischief is being done. It is understood that the Assessment Committees of Laheashire and other districts who complain that they are at a loss in levying local rates, on account of the uncertainty of the law and conflicting legal decisions as to the basis of rating, will ask the Government to receive a deputation from them on this subject on the 21st July.. The Government will do well to let it be known that they have no sympathy with any new departure which will cripple industry. If machi- nery s to be specially rated, why not put a tax on the workman's tools? It would be a similar absurdity.

Chairmen of Quarter Sessions are recognising that the licensing question has entered unon a new Phase. On Tuesday Mr. Fowler, addres- sing the grand jury at Cardiff, referred to the decision in Sharpe v. Wakefield. He held that there was an excess of licensed houses, but urged the magis- trates in weeding them out to exercise judicious and judicial discretion. A similar view was taken by Sir Horatio Lloyd, at the Chester Quarter sessions, on Monday. What is to be done in the boroughs in this district? The magistrates should take time by the forelock, and post themselves With such information as will enable them to dis- eharge their duties fairly and efficiently.

Now that the Warrington Water Works are 4bout to pass into the possession of the Corpora- tion, anglers are asking what arra-ngements will be /nade for permitting fishing in Walton Reservoir. SO. far as we can learn, there will be no change . 'existing arrangements. There was a time when _permission was given to the public to try their luck at Walton ; but this seems to have been dis- tasteful to Sir Gilbert Greenall. He therefore Acquired control of the fishing, and fishing so far as the public were concerned was immediately Stopped. Why should an ordinary angler come between the wind and his nobility ? There was a ziPlrpir.iise, during the election campaign, that per- issi.on to fish should be given on payment of a nominal fee; but this permission is accorded to a very, very limited number. As the matter stands,
the ratepayers of Warrington will not be able to fish in their own Reservoir.
