div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

*** New Tale! New Tale ! ! In our next.issue a new tale will be commenced entitled : " Lgetitia Thornton," from the pen of Louisa Bigg. It is a remarkable love story, well written, and so drawn as to retain the interest of the reader from beginning to end. RUNCORN PUBLIC HALL COWANY.

The directors of this Company, of whom Mr. John Brundrit J.P., is chairman, have appointed gtr. Gilbert Hitchmough of Sutherland-st., hall keeper in the pine of Mr. Thomas Saunders, resigned. " CAMDEN CHOIR EXCURSION, RUNCORN. "

The choir and friends of Camden Wesleyan Chapel, about 40 in number held an excursion on Saturday. They were conveyed to Chester in two brakes supplied by Messrs. Yarwood Bros., and a most enjoyable and pleasant day was spent in the ancient city, which was fully explored.

div.head: CARRYING FIREARMS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CARRYING FIREARMS AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, a youth named John Hughes was charged with having on the 24th May, carried and used a gun without having a license in force under the Gun Licensing Act, 1870. Mr. Moore, super- visor of Inland Revenue, prosecuted. On Sunday after- nom P.C. Worth found the defendant firing a pistol in a quarry at the Stone Hills. He had in his possession some powder and square pieces of lead. There were a number of children in the neighbourhood and it was dangerous to fire the pistol. The magistrates said ths boy had evidently acted in ignorance and he would be fined 6d. and costs, 9s. 6d.

OBSTRUCTION BY A RUNCORN TRADESMAN. On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Mendel Blank, furniture dealer, Bridge-st., was summoned for having on Saturday, the 20th June, obstructed the free passage of Bridge-st., by allowing two dozen chairs to remain there an unreasonable time.—P.S. Gosling proved the case.—Mr. Humphreys who defended said the defendant was a Jew and it was contrary to the practice of the Jews to do any work on their Sabbath until the sun had gone down. At seven o'clock, when the Sergeant drew the attention of the father of the defendant to the obstruction it was at once removed.—The Chairman said this was defendant's second offence; he must pay a fine of ss. and costs.
ASSAULT ON A POLICEMAN AT WIDNES.

At the Widnes Police Court on Monday, James Brett, 91, Midwood-street, was charged with assaulting and resisting P.C. Palmer. The constable stated that at half-past nine, on Saturday night, he took the prisoner's brother into custody for creating a breach of the peace. Prisoner demanded his brother's release. Witness refused to let him go,whereupon prisoner kicked him about the.legs and attempted to throw him down several times. Police .Constables Read and Hall and SergeantlMcCracken came to his assistance. Prisoner, who had been twice previously convicted, was commit- ted to gaol for fourteen days, without/ the option of a fine.

div.head: ASSAULTING THE POLICE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ASSAULTING THE POLICE AT RUNCORN.

Patrick Usher, a middle-aged man, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. Hughes. The Constable said he was in High-st., at 11•30 on Sunday night, when he heard a female voice screaming. He went to Mersey-st. and there saw the prisoner, who was only wearing his shirt and trousers, abusing a woman. He threatened to serve the officer in the same way, and when he was taken into custody he struck Use officer many times on the body. After a long struggle prisoner was taken to the Police Station, where he refused to be searched, and attempted to escape. The constable had a five minutes' struggle to put the prisoner in the cell. He was very drunk. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed in each case or 14 days.

div.head: ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN PUBLICAN.
div.p: ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN PUBLICAN.

John Salt and Frederick Shell, young men, were brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday to answer a charge of assaulting Wm. Hughes, landlord of the Commercial Hotel (Glass Barrel). Hughes refused to serve the men with drink and ordered them to leave, not 'because they were drunk but because he had had some annoyance with Salt three months previously. They refused and he ejected them. They returned and attacked him, one kicking him while he lay on the ground. Hughes did not deny that he had used a window pole in the scuffle with the men.—Mr. James Reynolds said the land- lord was in the wrong in ejecting men, from his house for an offence committed threemonths ago, but the de- fendants had taken the law into their own hands and must each pay a fine of ss. and costs.
UNJUST _SCAIES AND WEIGHTS AT WIDNES.

Rebecca Locker, greengrocer of Warrington, was sum- moned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of having In her possession weights and scales which were unjust.—lnspector Kilpatrick said on Satur- day he saw a cart belonging to the defendant in Kent-st., Widnes. It was loaded with potatoes and was in charge of a hired servant. He found on the cart a pair of scales which were 18 drachms against the purchaser, a 71b. weight 4 drachms light, and a 41b. weight, 1O drachms light.—The defendant pleaded guilty to the weights being light but the scales were not her property and she had not seen them before,but the man had gone away,and she could not call him to prove her assertion. The weights she had sent a few days previously to be adjusted by the borough inspector of Warrington but he was unable to do then-I.—The magistrates said she ought not to have sent the weights out under those circumstances and she must pay the costs. For using the unjust scales she would be fined 10s. and costs.

INSPECTION OF POLICE AT WIDNES. The annual Government inspection of the Widnes Police Force took took place on Thursday afternoon. The inspecting officer was the Hon. Captain Legge, who was accompanied by Colonel Moorsom, the chief Coastable of the county, and a thorough examination in every detail was made. There were on parade Supt. Noblett, In- spector Keighley, and Inspector Kilpatrick (weights and measures)' six sergeants and 30 constables. There were absent on duty one sergeant, and six constables and one was sick. After Captain Legge had examined clothing and accoutrements of the men, they went through a number of evolutions of drill in creditable style. The single men's quarters, and the cells of the police station were visited and examined, and then the office- books and the duty books of the sergeants and con- stables were examined. Fnally the Inspector expressed himself highly satisfied with the result of his visit, every thing having been found in the most complete order. • A FAMILY SQUABBLE AT RUNCOR.

Sarah Ann Reese, a married woman, of Weston, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting Mary Ann Jones. A cross summons had been issued.—Mr. Burton appeared for Mrs. Jones and Mr. Humphreys for Mrs. Reese.—Mrs. Jones said she was the wife of George Edwin Jones and had lived at 49, Rutland-st. Mrs. Reese who was her sister-in-law, and her mother-in-law, called at her house on Tuesday afternoon the 22nd June' and some conver- sation took place about her husband being lazy. Mrs. Reese said she was killing him by inches and used some strong language. he ordered her out, and Mrs. Reese then struck her in the face. Her husband then held her while Mrs. Reese pinched her on the head and face.—By Mr. 'Humphreys: All the furniture had been sold and her husband was living with Mrs. Reese.—lnspector Bowyer said Mrs. Jones came to the police office and she was bleeding from a wound on the face.—Mr. Humphreys called Mrs. Reese, who said she asked her brother how it was he was not at work and he replied "Jam lazy" and Mrs. Jones stated "I said lie was lazy." Mrs. Jones struck the first blow and she struck her back in self defence. Her brother separated them, and did not hold his wife.—ln cross-examination Mrs. Reese said she told Mrs. Jones that she was filling her belly, and clemmil-g..r her husband. She was killing him by inches. The hus- band said to her "Give it her Nance" and she did do, and she could give it her again if she wanted it. When the furniture was sold she brought a stick into the street and shouted " hurrah" but it was because Mrs. Jones had got a lot there to hoot.—The mother-in-law having given evidence, the Bench dismissed both cases,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 4, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 4, 1891.
A STURGEON CAPTURED AT WESTON Poiyr,

-- -----___ A number of canal workers caught a sturgeon at Weston Point on Saturday ilast, and reaped a harvest by exhibit- ing the royal fish n Runcorn. It was afterwards re- tailed by Mr. George Duckett, and there were numerous eager purchasers. .
HEAVY RAINFALL AT RUNCORN.

A very heavy fall of rain occurred at Runcorn, on Wednesday afternoon, and the railway line at Flalton Junction was flooded to a depth of three feet. The Bris- tol express was detained some time in consequence. A gang of men cut channels to allow the water to escape, and the line was quickly comparatively clear.

MUTE OF A RUNCORN LADY. On Sunday the wife of the Rev. Joseph C. Harrop, a gentleman well-known in Frodsham, died at the resi- dence of her husband in Luton, where he is engaged in the Wesleyan ministry. She was a native of Runcorn, and was the daughter of the late Mr. C. Kent, of that town.

div.head: MILKING COWS ON THE MARSH AT WIDNES:
div.p: MILKING COWS ON THE MARSH AT WIDNES:

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, John Dugg- an, (13), of Church-st.' and Walter Cowley, (11), of Lugsdale road, were charged with stealing a quantity of milk. Complaints having been frequently made to the police that boys were in the habit of milking cows on the Marsh, two constables were set to watch and on Monday they saw the defendants follow the cows, and bring one to a standstill. They then milked the animal for about three minutes and drank the milk. The boys pleaded guilty and were each ordered to receive six strokes of the birch rod. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE..

A meeting of the Widnes Free Library Committed was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday afternoon, pre- sided over by Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P. The members present were—Messrs. D. J. Brooks, W. Sadler, S. Hoyle (accountant), and the Clerk. The librarian's re- port for the month of June was read and adopted. The question of providing a room for boys was again dis- cussed, but it was eventually deferred until the Local Board have confirmed the estimate of the probable cost of the structure. It was also decided to allow the lib- rarian the usual summer holidays, and that Miss Robin- son be engaged as substitute during their absence. THE FATAL ACCIDENT TO A BOY AT WIDNES. The Deputy-coroner, Mr. W. T. Husband, on Monday, held an inquest at Widnes Accident Hospital, on the body of Edward Wright, aged 14, son of Richard Wright, labourer, Brown-st. The deceased was a soap cutter at the works.of Messrs. Gossage and Sons, and on Thurs- day evening, deceased and another boy named William Cank got into the hoist, while a boy named Henry Ditch- field commenced to heave up. When the hoist had passed through the first 110 or and part of the next, Cank jumped out and deceased stopped in. Some one below shouted. "Lower the hoist," and Ditchfield did so Deceased then made a jump to get out,and the gate fell on him. He was badly hurt about the back, and he was at once conveyed to the Hospital and attended by Dr. McDonnell. He died on Friday night. The evi- dence showed that the boys had no right to meddle with the hoist.—A verdict of Accidental death" was re- turned.

ROBBERY OF RABBITS AT DITTO;i. At the Widnes Police Court on Monday, Thomas Cauge, Halebank-road, Ditton., was charged in custody with stealing two tame rabbits, valued at is. Bd., the property of James Catto, on the 21 June. The prosecu- tor identified the rabbits as his property, and said he missed them between nine o'clock on the night of the 21st June, and nine o'clock on the morning of the 22nd. They were worth is. Bd. Prisoner lived about 100 yards from his house, and on Sunday he went with P.C. Townley to prisoner's house, where he found the rabbits. —James Daglish, of Halebank, said the rabbits were the same he sold to the prosecutor about three weeks ago. P.C. Townley stated that prisoner said he had bought the rabbits in the market.—Mary Hulme, grocer and general dealer, Ann-st. West, Said she had a stall in the market, and sold rabbits; no one else sold'rabbits in the market besides her. She never sold the rabbits produced to the prisoner.—Superintendent Noblett : We have offered to do everything we can to help him to produce the man from whom he alleges he purchasedithe rabbits.—The Chairman said the Bench considered that the case was pretty clearly proved, and that the rabbits belonged to the prosecutor. Prisoner would be fined 205., or go to prison for 14 days.

div.head: HIGH LEGH CHURCH.
div.p: HIGH LEGH CHURCH.

It is stated that the above church, which was re- cently burned down, will be re-built on the old site, it being considered that if new foundations were laid elsewhere, it would involve an expendi-. ture of at least £4OO more. THE SUMMER STEAMSHIP SERVICE TO THE ISLE

OF MAN. The arrangements of the Isle of Nlan Steam Packet Company with regard to their summer service bet- ween Liverpool,Douglas,and Ramsey are now com- pleted, and the programme will be found to indi- cate a very careful consideration of the convenience of visitors,to the charming Manx resorts. The first- class steamer of the company will leave Liv rpool for the island every week-day at 11.30 a.m. and 4 p.m. Steamers will leave Douglas for Liverpool ehch week-day at 9 a.m.,!and 4 p.m. The boats will go to Ramsey every week-day except Friday.

div.head: VIOLENT APPRENTICES AT ST. lIELENS.
div.p: VIOLENT APPRENTICES AT ST. lIELENS.

John Johnson, 128, Peter-st., an apprentice in the employ of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, glass manu- facturers, was summoned at the Town Hall, on Monday, for assaulting William Gladstone Blake, one of the foremen, and the firm applied for an order rescinding the apprenticeship indentures. Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted, and the evidence showed that the defendant and another boy named Morgan had repeatedly struck Blake. Morgan had since apologised and expressed his intention never to repeat the offence, but the defendant would do neither. He was fined 10s. and costs for the assault, and the indentures were cancelled. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: LANCASHIRE COUNTY FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COUNTY FOOTBALL CLUB.

A Committee--------- of the Lancashire County Football Club was held at the Grand Hotel, Man- chester, on Monday night, when a division was made of the profits of the Lancashire V. :Rest of England match. The net proceeds came to £B5O, and the money was divided as follows :—Manches- ter Royal Infirmary £lOO, Salford Hospital £95, Children's Hospital £5O, Southern Hospital £5O, Ancoats Dispensary £5O, Wigan Infirmary £5O, Oldham Infirmary £5O, Skin Hospital £5O, Liver- pool Infirmary £2O, Warrington Infirmary £l5, St. Helens Infirmary £l5, Dental Hospital £2O, Sick Nurses' Institution £lO, Adult Deaf and Dumb £lO, Hospitable for Incurables £l5. Tlid only county matches at present arranged are those with Cheshire and Yorkshire. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. TRY: HOME IRON TRADE. ,The outlook in the English iron market continues unpromising, business being practically stagnant, and the near approach of the holiday season pre- cludes all hope of a speedy improvement. Transac- tions in the Glasgow warrant market are very scarce. Both Cleveland and Bessemer pig are fi rm in price, but the demand is very slow. In finished iron prices are rather firmer than they have been lately, but prices are still unremunerative. In tin- plates there is a steady tone observable, but en- quiries are. very limited. The majority of makers have closed their works for the month. There is very little business stirring in the steel trade, but prices are steadily upheld. New orders in the shipbuilding and engineering trades are still want- ing, and in the coal trade only a quiet tone is re- ported.—li

B IRKB ECK BUILDING SOCIETY. The 40th annual meeting of the Birkbeck Build- ing Society was held en Tuesday at the offices, 29 and 30, Southampton Buildings, Chancery-lane. The report adopted, states that the receipts during the year which ended 31st March last reached £9,519,070 making a total from the commencement of the society of more than one hundred and forty millions (£141,766,177.) The deposits received were £7,093,047 and the subscriptions £244,927. The gross profits amounted to £284,315. The surplus funds have been augmented by £244,167 and now stand at £5, 098,507, of which £1,628,240 is invested in con- sols and other securities guaranteed by the British , Government,and the cash in the hands of the bankers is £317,929. A further sum of £25,000 has been added to the permanent guarqnteefund, thus bring- ing up the amount to £150,000, and the balance £134,315 making together .£284,315, in excess of the liabilities, the whole a.niount being invested in consols. The subscriptions and deposits withdraw- able on demand amount to £5,247,712.. The 13th triennial bonus on investing shares has been allotted and the amount placed to the credit of all shares in existence at the close of the 40th year is £33,033. The surplus funds (which are invested in readily convertible securities) are sufficient to pay the de- positors 114 per cent. on the amount ot their de- posits. The new accounts opened during the year were 10,051, and there are, altogether, 60,045 share- holders and depositors on the books. Since its establishment, the society has returned to the shareholders and depositors more than one hundred millions (t 117,071.323 the whole amount having, been repaid upon demand.

div.head: MARRIAGE QUESTION AT ST. BELENS.
div.p: THE MARRIAGE QUESTION AT ST. BELENS.

At the St. Helens Police Court oa Monday, James Thomason, of Kenyon, was summoned for deserting his wife, Rose. -Mr. J. O. Swift appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Buckley, of Leigh, for the decendant. It appeared that the parties had been married for over two years, and there was one child. The complainant alleged that her husband had thrashed her and deserted her on the 16th inst. They were then living at St. Helens, and he was employed at the Pheenix-Colliery.—Mr. Buckley,for the defence, said in that case the husband provided a home and asked his wife to live with him,' but if she thought proper, like a notable case recently before the country, to walk away to a home of her own, they shculd let her fight for herself. They could not ask a man to conform in evel'y respect to the whims and fancies of a woman who did not care a straw for him. He submitted that no deser- tion had been proved.—The bench ultimately made an order for the payment of 7s. 6d. per week. LAWN MOWEP.S.—Garland, 51. Bridge-st., Warrington. and at Earlestown.—Adrt.
THE N lair BAPTIST 'MINISTER FOR EARLESTOWN

On Saturday night a public gathering was held in the Jubilee Baptist Church, Boundary-road, St. Helens, on the occasion of the departure of the Rev. J. Cottam, pastor, to take charge of the Baptist Church at Earlestown. The reverend gentleman succeeded the Rev. C. Green at Boundary-road four years ago, and the congregation expressed their. appreciation of his services by presenting to him on Saturday night, through the senior deacon (Mr. J. Abercrombie), a handsomely framed illustrated address, which testified to the esteem in which Mr. Cottam was held and the regret which was felt at the loss of his services. Mr. John Leith qccupied the chair, and addresses were given by the Revs. J. Brown (Presbyterian), M. Lewis (Liverpool), H. W. Ayres, F.S.Sc. (Park-road), and R. J. Ward Congre- gational.) The Rev. J. Cottam, in acknowledging the receipt of the testimonial, thanked them for the expression of their kindly feelings, and said he hoped the church at Boundary-road would continue to prosper. 6113131311 Fasmoss now Showing at 04 a. W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt.

SALE AT "BROOKSIDE" NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS. On Thursday week Messrs.J: B. and B. Leaeh,of St. Helens,conducted a sale of the above house in which great interest was manifested. The bidding was very spirited and good prices were obtained. Silver realised up to 235. 3d. per oz. The highest price realised for engravings of which, there was a valu- able collection was 54 guineas for the "Monarch of the Olen" after Landseer. A small oil painting by Crosby sold fer 14 guiLeas. The appointments in the various entertaining rooms and bed chambers fetched good prices, and amongst the sums got for the books were Waverley novels £4 15s. 10d., Lever's Works £6, Thackeray's Works £6 155., Ingoldsby Legends £4.—On Tuesday last Mr. Leach submitted to public auction at the Pied Bull Inn, Newtoti, the estate which comprises the residence, known as Brookside, Newton-le-Aillows, lately occupied by J. H. Birley,Esq., J.P.,now deceased,with the stabling, Orden, lawn tennis. &c. The bidding commenced at £5OO, and the property was finally knocked down to Mr. Alderman Smith, J.P., of Wigan for £1,030. Messrs. Robert Davies & Co., were the vendors' solicitors.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse. Mr. Mclntyre presided,and there were present Rev. J. W. N. Tanner. Messrs. Knowles, S. Taylor, Aaron, Lea, Lewis, Bretherton, Parr, Ed- wards, W. Whitlow, Ashton (clerk)
INFLUENZA IN THE HOUSE.

In accordance with a request from the Local Govern- ment Board, Dr. Robinson, medical officer to the Work- house, prepared a report on the.outbreak of influenza in the House., The disease originated through a tramp ad- mitted on the 4th May. The next patient was Margaret Jackson then followed the master (Mr. Cunnah), and the disease went through the House. There was a total of 35 cases and seven deaths occurred. There were five patients still under treatment.
REMUNERATION FOR SERVICES:

It was resolved to pay Mr. H. G. Linaker £l2 10s., for his services as acting clerk from the date of his father's death, March 16th until the 21st April; this amount to cover his attendance at the audit.

div.head: REDUCING EXPENDITURE.
div.p: REDUCING EXPENDITURE.

Mr. Brandreth moved the passing of accounts amount- ing to £BOl 18s. 11d. He was pleased to say that as compared with the corresponding quarter last year these accounts showed a decrease of £lOO, and the master had informed the Committee that his stock of food and of raiment in the House was greater than it was last June. The expenditure on butcher's meat had been £2O less ; grocery, £l7 less ; drngs, £6 les4 ; coke, £8 less; coal, £8 less ; drapery. £l6 less ; making th expenditure for the quarter about £lOO less than the corresponding quarter last year. The balance in treasurer's hands was £4,053 10s. sd.—Mr. Edwards seconded the motion, which was carried.
TIEN_ COUNTY COUNCIL AG:ILN

Mr. Aaron said in the " Liverpool Courier" of the 24th June there was a report, of the meeting -of the Guardians of Birkenhead at which the Chairman stated the county rate for the half-year was £2,617 19s. 9d., as compared with £2,600 in the previous ball year; an increase of £l7. Now in the Runcorn Union the County call was between .4300 and £BOO more than in the previous half year. Could the Chairman explain how this difference in the calls of the two unions arose.—The Chairman: I cannot tell you.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner: Better ask the County Council.—The Chairman: I think we shall have to send Mr. Aaron to the County Council to represent us.—Mr. Aaron: I cannot understand it; rthink it wants explanation.—Mr. Edwards said he thought the explanation was that Birkenhead was a borough,and boroughs were excluded from the control of the Council.—Mr. Aaron did not think that fully explained the matter.—Mr. Whitlow: Tbey have heard you rattling at them and have increased the call of Runcorn Union.— Mr. Edwards: They 'want more rattling at. The County Council is a body framed for the spending of money and nothing else.—Mr. Aaron: I move that the Clerk write to the Clerk to the County Council and ask for an ex- ,: planation.—Mr. Edwards seconded.—Mr. Taylor: Have ! you an answer to the last inquiry? (Laughter.)—The ,! Clerk: No, not yet. (Laughter.) Will you wait until we ! get an answer to that.—Mr. Parr (decidedly) No, no. (Laughter.)—Mr..Aaron said the difference was so glaring he must press his motion. If they would not give answers to their inquiries, he would write to the Hope Secretary. and tell him.—The motion was carried unanimously.
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. _ _

The fortnighly --meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tudsday. Mr. Mclutvre presided, and there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Aaron, Knowles, Edwards; Brandreth, and J. Ashton (clerk), and J. Farrington (nuisance in- spector.
THE SHIP CANAL AND SEWERAGE.

Mr. L. W. Wells,- engineer to the Authority, wrote stating that he had taken an office copy of the agreement with the Manchester Ship Canal Co., and also a copy of each plan. A substantial subway wai being built at Apple- ton, to contain the" Twenty Step "sewer, which would be passed through an iron pipe in accordance with the agreement. 18 inch cast iron pipes were on the ground at Frodsham for the sewer outfall and ten of them were laid across the mid-feather between the two depositing tanks. He inspected this yesterday and he called at the engineers office as to certain details.

VYRNWY WATER, The Inspector said he had received a fetter from Mr. Evans, agent to Norton Estate, stating that negotiations were proceeding with the Liverpool Corporation to supply Yew Tree Farm with Vyravry water. NEW HOUSES. The plans of three houses at Stockton Heath, for Mr. John Hedgceck, were approved. THE PLAGUE OF BONES AT FRODSHAM. Mr. H. S. Chapman, of Sanclow. Frodsham, wrote as follows :—" I must again call your attention to the abominable nuisance from putrid bones at Frodsham station. I was quite ill this morning from the stench, and it is quite impossible to even walk in the garden in consequence without retching. Something must be done to stop it or we shall all get bloodpoisoning. Why can- not the trucks be taken to same small station where there are no residential inhabitants and the trucks disin- fected before carting. I think the Sanitary Authority will have a good deal to answer for should an epidemic break out; and no drinking water in a town the size of Frodsham I think a disgrace—Mr. Aaron said the last time a complaint was mane he inspected the bones and found them to consist of fresh cows heads' which when he was a boy would have been bought for the purpose of making broth. At that time there was no nuisance whatever.l—Tbe Inspector said the Railway Company had been very obliging In the matter. If the bones ar- rived on a Saturday they were taken to Helsby, (laughter)—where there was plenty ot space. In mov-

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

Dr. McDougall, medical of health,reported that during June there were 35 deaths, of which three wore inquest cases, and of the remaining 32. 5 were due to convul- sions, 4 to phthisis pulmonalis, 2 to w;asoping cough, 4 to bronchitis, 4 to mesenterid. disease, 4 to inflammation of the lungs, 2 to parturition, and one each to influenza, cancer, paralysis, malformation of mouth,heart disease, blood disease, efftnion of Wood on the brain, and kidney disease. The 35 deaths showed an avefoge death rate for the twelve months of 21 per 1,000 of tlio estimated population and exclusive of the inquest cases of 19.2. The authority would be glad to hear that the town was practically free from infectious disease.—The surveyor said in the corresponding month last year there wete 28 deaths.—ln answer to Mr. Hankinson, Dr. McDougall said there was only on,e or two cases of influenza in the town. He had had no notifications of infectious disease during June, but two cases of scarlet fever were notified on the previous day. The health of the town was exceptionally good.—The report was con- sidered highly satisfactory.
WORK IN COMMITTEE.

On the recommendation of the Buildings Committee the plan of six cottages in Grosvenor-st., for Mr. Chas. Nickson were approved. On the recommendation of the Health Committee it was decided that notices be served on the following persons to abate nuisances aris- ing from over7crowding,and in the event of non-compli- ance that legal proceedings be taken :—George Dutton, 37, Masori-st. ; William Wainwright, Back Mersey-st ; Robert: Rawlinson, Salkeld-Spuare ; Michael Mulherne, 10, Alcock-st. ; that Thomas Parry, 23, Albert-st., be registered as a Purveyor of Milk; that notice be served on Mr. George Davidson, Church-st.,to abate a nuisance arising from the melting of fat The Finance Committee reported that during the month the treasurer had received the following sums: General district rate £371 18s. id.; market rents and tolls £3O 4s. 9d; slaughter houses &c. £4 13s. 9d.; total £406 16s. 7d. Accounts amounting to £668 ss. 9d. on general fund; £4l 11s. id. on loan account and £25 33. 7d. on library fund were passed for payment. During June £371 18s. id. of the general district rate had been col- lected, and there was a balance of £2,148 10s. 8& to be collected.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Present Board of Guardians was held at Whiston Workhouse on Thursday afternoon, when there were present Mr. J. Burchall (chairman), Rey. S. A. K. Sylvester and Dean Finegan, Messrs. F. Stapleton-Bretherton, .1.P., Johnson, Lowe, Middlehurst, Hulme, Goldsworth, Wareing, Ranson, Davies, Peover, Daine, Kenwright, Joseph Birchall, E. Birehall, W. E. Longton, Mercer, Buckley, Griffiths and A. F. Mann (clerk.) RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported that the number of inmates this week was 545, last week 511, corresponding week last year 476; vagrants relieved 9.2, last week 42. A COMPLAINT FROM THE AUDITOR.— The Local Government Board wrote enclosing an extract from a report which they had received from the district auditor relative to the accounts for the half year ended at Lady Day last, of Mr. Joseph Treacy, late receiving officer for Widnes. The auditor complained about the omission of necessary particulars in the relieving officer's books. The Clerk stated that he had forwarded a copy of the instructions and of the auditor's remarks to the officers.

MR NEW CLERIC—The Local Government Board wrote on the 23rd June assenting to the appointment of Mr. A.F. Mann,as Clerk to the Guardians, and approving of the salary of £3OO per annum.—The Clerk submitted the bond for £5OO into which he had entered for the ful- filment of his duties. Tuti VACANCIES ON THE BOARD.—The Clerk reported the receipt of orders from the Local Government Board for special elections of Guardians for the townships of Bold, Prescot and Whiston. The Clerk said the usual notices had been issued.

AGED MARRIED COUPLES IN TIIE NORKHOUSE.—The Local Government Board-wrote on 29th June stating that in a report received from their assistant inspector, Mr. Morrison, of his visit to the Workhouse on the llth inst., he informed them that two aged couples hai informed him that they were desirous of liring together.—The Local Government Board desired to draw attention that section 23 of the 10th and 11th Victoria provided that aged married persons received into the Workhouse, both of whom were above the age of 60 years, should not be compelled to live seperate and apart from each other in ' the Workhouse.—The Clerk reported that the require- ments of both couples had now been complied with. THE LATE CLERK.—On the recommendation of the Assessment Committee it was decided to allow Mrs. Har- tley, widow to the late clerk to the Board and the Com- mittee, the sum of £9O, as the proportion of salary due to the late Mr. Hartley. Mr. Middlehurst seconded the .; motion, which was adopted.

DRIINKENNESS.—John-M—ceor—MiCk: no fixed residence ; James Keogh, Ditton ; Catherine Carroll, no fixed resi- dence ;Richard D. 805c0w,43, Pleasant-st. ; Thos. Brett, L 3, Nelson-st. ; George Simpson, Mary Glynn, and Mary Treacy, all of Nelson-st. ; and Johtt Ilegarty, Rainhill; were each fined ss. and cists for being drunk and dis- orderly. BREACH OF THE PRAcx.-4-Patrick Brett, 19, Midwood- st., was charged with creating a breach of the peace by fighting on some waste land near Lugsdale-road, shortly after nine o'clock on Saturday night, and was bound over to keep the peace for three months, or go to gaol for seven days.—llizabeth Bonnen, 15, Warrington-road, was charged with a like offence by P.C. Cummins, and was similarly dealt with. Tnurr o Con. ny BOys.—Wra. James Rimmer, 15, Pleasant-st. (13), and Samuel Pope, les Pleasant-st., (10), were Charged with stealing about 10lbs. of coal from the London and NorthiWestern railway siding off Lugsdale-road, Widnes, on Snnday, about noon.—P.C. Davies deposed to seeing the lads climb over a wall by means of a ladder and fetch the coal from the siding.— Rimmer was ordered to receive eight strokes, and. Pope six strokes of the birch rod,
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies.

KNIFE on PIPE STEM ?—Two sailors named James Thomas and Bob Wheat,were charged with using threats to Richard Abram Houghton, a young man. Prosecutor said at half-past twelve on Saturday night he saw the defendants and two or three ether sailors molesting a girl on Waterloo Bridge. He told them to go on board their vessel, and one made a prod at him with a knife. Be shouted to a man, and the sailors ran away.—Maria Rawlinson, the girl in question,did not appear.—The de- fendants said the prosecutor pretended to lee a detective, and one of the party pretended to draw a knife, but it was really a pipe stem. As there was no corroboration, 1 the case was dismissed. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence, a fine of ss. and costs was imposed on John Johnson,Henry Lever,John Thorpe Elizabeth Barker, Jessie Wood, Mary Ann Gittens, Thos. Baker, and James Marshall; Philip Taylor and Samuel Finch, summoned on a similar charge, were dismissed. Mr. Burton defended. cIiIIELTY TO A HORSE.—Abraham Naylor, a boatman, was summoned for cruelly ill-treating a horse, by work- ing it while in an unfit state, and on the evidence of an inspector of the R.S.P.C. A., he was fined is. and costs, 6d. STREET OBSTRUCTION.—WiIIiam Prescott,a young man, was fined 6d. and costs, for obstructing the footpath in Bridge-st., by loitering there. TIIREAT.—Henry Busker was charged with using Oreats to Benjamin Taylor, and he was bound over to keep the peace for six months. IlincsNcy.—Jane Ellison and Thomas Kennedy, were charged with indecent conduct at Belvedere on Saturday , night, and A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon each defendant, AN UNtAciaNsan ElAwircn.—For hawking withont al license Robert Evans was fined 53. and costs or seven days. ASSAULT.—Martin O'Neil and John Kilgrass was charged with assaulting John Clarke, in Weston-road, on Saturday,and were each fined ss. and costs. Clarke was walking out with his sweetheart when the defend- ants met him and assatffted him.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

DEATH OF MR. PETER POTTER.—Mr. Peter Potter died at the residence of his grandson at Croft, on Saturday evening. The deceased, who was 72 years of age, was a, highly respected farmer, and his death will be much re- gretted by a large circle of friends. The funeral took place in Padgate churchyard on Wednesday afternoon. Sr. LEWIS'S R.C.CueeEL.—The annual sermons in aid of the day and Sunday schools in connection with St Lewis's Roman Catholic Chapel, Croft, took place on Sunday. There were large congregations, and the musical portions of the services were rendered by the choir in a praise- worthy manner. Mr. William Battersby was at the organ. The Rev. F. Monaghan conducted the first part of the service, including mass, and two sermons were preached by the Rev. F. Bede, 0.P., of Sutton, near St. Helens, who made appeals at both services for subscrip- tions.= behalf of the schools. Good collections were made. CHRIST CHURCH SERMONS.—Ihe annual s4rmon3 on behalf of the Sunday school and choir were preached on Sunday, at Christ Church, in the morning by the Rector, and in the evening by the Rev. J.J. Langharn, M.A., vicar of Padgate. There were large congrega- tions. The services were choral, and special anthems were sung' namely, "Make a joyful noise unto the Lord, all ye lands" (Caleb Simper), and "I will always give thanks unto the Lord." Mr. W. C. Savage was at the organ. The prayers were read in the morning by the Rector, who also preached, and Captain Withington, of Culcheth, read the lessons. The collections amounted to £lO 17s.

div.head: FRODSHAM. ,
div.p: FRODSHAM. ,

LOCAL CASES AT THB QUARTER SESSIONS.—At the Chester Quarter Sessions, on Monday, George Robinson, jun., (22), labourer, was charged with stealing £lB, the money of George Robinson, farm labourer, Kingsley, on the Ist May. Prisoner was seen to enter his father's house, and afterwards it was found that a drawer had been broken open, and £lB extracted from £4l which had been saved by the prosecutor.—Prisoner was found guilty, and a Police Sergeant who gave "his character" said he was a notorious tooacher, an associate of thieves, and a disgrace to his father, who was a,most respectable and hard-working man.—Six month's hard labour.— Jonathan Hewitt, (20), collier, was charged with assault- ing Mary Ellams, four yeas of age, at Frodshani. on the 19th May.—He was committed to prison for two calender months with hard labour.

MARRIAGE OF REV. A. 11. WALKER, B.A.—On Tues- day, Clapton Lodge. Halifax, was the scene of much ani- mation, owing-to the marriage of Miss Annie Clegg, second daughter of Mr. Councillor Clegg, to the Rev. A. H. Walker, B. A., assistant tutor at Didsbury College, son of Mr. S. Walker, of Frodsham. The ceremony took place in the afternoon, at the Rhodes-st., Wesleyan Chapel, in the presence of a crowded assembly of relatives and friends, the ceremony being performed by the Rev. R. Green and the Rev. Dr. Randles, of Didsbury College. The bridesmaids were the two sisters of the bride, and Miss Walker, sister of the bridegroom, whilst the Rev. J. A. Ingle, M.A., of the Leys School, Cambridge, was the best man. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a dress of ivory faille with chiffon embroidery and ruche, and a tulle veil with natural flowers. The Rhodes-st. choir were present, and during the service sang " The voice that breathed o'er Eden," and "0, love divine and golden." Mr. Catherall ably presided at the organ. The wedding presents were very numerous and costly, and included one from the Rhodes-st:, Wesleyan choir and another from the teachers and scholars in con- nection with the Sunday School. In the afternoon a re- ception was held at ClapOn Lodge, and later in the day the couple left for London, en route for Switzerland. ' where the honeymoon is to be spent.

div.head: – THE PROPOSED LOCAL RAILWAY.
div.p: - THE PROPOSED LOCAL RAILWAY.

The Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Rail- way Bill, which authorises the construction of a trunk line across England from Warrington on the west, passing by way of Macclesfield, Bux- ton, Chesterfield, and Lincoln, to Sutton-on-Sea on the east coast, came, on Thursday. before a Select Committee of the House of Lords, pre- sided over by Lord Basing. It will be recollected that after an exhaustive inquiry the measure passed the House of Commons, but with the omission of certain running powers which were asked for. The promoters were represented by Mr. Pope, Q.C., Mr. Pember, Q.C., Mr. Pembroke Stephens, QC.. Mr. Batten, Mr. Banks, and Mr. L. M. Richards; whilst the opponents appearing were represented as fol- lows; Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, by Mr. Littler. Q.C., Mr. Worsley Taylor, Q.C.. and Mr. A. S. Rickards; and Mr. Charles Stephen Leslie and others, by Mr. Cripps. Q.C., and Mr. Trevor. The Midland Railway Wmpany and the Cheshire Lines Committee also petitioned against the Bill, but reserved appearance by counsel. 'Mr. Pope, Q.C.' in opening the case for the promo- ters, said that the line was perhaps the largest and most important undertaking which had been before Parlia- ment for many years past, not only with regard to the amount of money which was involved in its construc- tion, but the extraordinary amount of interest and the influential character of the suppprt under which it was brought forward. It was a line which, being 16L miles of new line joined to ten already authorised, would ultimately make a new railway from the east to the west, involving a capital of 6. millions. The estimate for works was 44 millions, includ- ing the land. The promoters of the Bill have given the best evidence of their bona-fides, be- cause they had themselves found the depc6it, amounting to £220,000, which the standing orders of Parliament rendered necessary in the case of a new line. The pro- moters had also paid out of their own pockets the very large expense of the promotion of the Bill. He thought that certainly of late years no Bill had come before Parliament with such influential sanction and with so strong an amount of local support. It was, in fact, a scheme promoted by the whole of the landowners, trad- ers, and tenants interested from end to end, and the object was to associate together. those noble- men and gentlemen who hitherto having been dependent upon local efforts to develop their districts had found themselves tock weak to stand alone against the opposition of the great railway companies. With regard bp the present scheme; the only oppenents. ' were the M.S. and L., who wese at present the east and west coast railway, and a single landowner, Mr. Leslie. Every one else along the proposed line was enthusiasti- cally in favour of the scheme. He was afraid he should have to tax their lordships' patience whilst he put a great number of gentlemen into the box to state their wishes for the construction of the line. His difficulty in , the case was to deal with .a cloud of witnesses who were anxious to come and express their desires. He had a sheaf of names, but he could only say that he should exercise his right as conducting the case to hold a strong hand over those witnesses, and repress them as far as he was able rather than to occupy the committee's time to over- due length. Having briefly described the characteristics of the proposed line the learned counsel said that the names mentioned in the Bill as the first directors of the company were the Duke. of Newcastle, Lord Manvers, Lord Cilnton Hope, Mr. Bromley, Davenport, Mr. Ark- wright, Mr. DalrymNe, Mr. Jarvis, Mr. Nicholson, and Mr. Stanniforth, It was no speculators' Or contractors' line, but a hona-ilde landowners' and trade's line, intended to open up the Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire coalfield to the east and west coast. When the lines at present sanctioned in that district werecompleted, that coalfield, so far as southern traffic was concerned, would have the London and North-Wes- tern, the Midland and the Great Northern, and the Man- chester, Sheffield, and Lincoln serving it towards the Humber. .
Several witnessek ha.ving given evidence in favour of the Will, the committee adjourned until next day,

TF.ETERDAY'S EVIDENCE. The:House of Lords Select Committee met again—yes- terday morning, Lord Basing presiding, and heard fur- ther evidence in favour of the projected line from War- rington to Sutton-on-the-Sea. Among the witnesses was the Hon. A. de Tatton Egerton, M.P., for the Knutsford division who stated that his constituents attached great importance to the provision of better railway facilities betweeh Knutsford and Warrington on the west, and to Macclesfield and Derbyshire on the east. His father whose estate extended for six or seven miles along the proposed use, was distinctly in favour of the project. This concluded the landowners' evidence, and Mr. Jack- son, member of the firm of Fletcher and iCo., owners of the Claycruss Colleries, Derbyshire, was then called, among the other witnesses to speak of the value of the proposed line for the conveyance of coal between the Derbyshire fields and Cheshire.

The Bill will again come before the committee of the House of Lords,on Monday. It is expected that,on behalf of Warrington, evidence will be given in its support by the mayor (Alderman Francomb), the borough surveyor (Mr. Longdin), Mr. George Woods, of the Longfoxd Wire and Iron Company, and Mr. W. Carson, managing director of the 14 hitecross Coal and Iron Company.

div.head: TRIPS FROM. WARMICTOTO/1.
div.p: TRIPS FROM. WARMICTOTO/1.

As usual on the day after Walking Day, there were a number of works trips from Warrington on Saturday. One of the largest of these was that of the employes at the Whitecross Works which was to Blackpool. They were accompanied by a num- ber of tlw cPiployo of ..k§,§ra• T. Fletcher and Co., and of Messrs. Naylor, tiiiiber racrchaute., and num- bered in all about 1,350. The flrst train left Data Quay station at 6.50, and the second at 7.5, and in each case the popular watering .place was reached in good time. Rain marred the pledsure of the visitors, who visited the different objects of interest in the town and neighbourhood. The return journey was very disappoint- ing. One of the trains did not leave Blackpool until half-past nine, and, owing to obstructions on the way, Warrington was not reached till ten minutes to one on Sunday morning. The Committee wish those who accompanied them to Blackpool to understand that the delay did not rest with them. Mr. Samuel Dunbobbin acted as secretary to the Trip Committee. Messrs. Crosfield's w.rkmen had a tripto Llandudno, between 600 and 700 of the men starting for that place from Bank Quay station early in the morning. The weather was wet fora short time after they reached their destination, but soon cleared up, and the remainder of the day was fine; and after having had a very pleasure- able time, the workmen left Llandudno about half-past seven reaching home about ten o'clock. Mr. W. H. Robinson was secretary of the trip. Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., gave their men a trip to Southport, and they started, to the number of about 425,fr0m the Central Station at ten minutes past B,reach- ing Southport about 9. After a very enjoyable day they left that place about t2n minutes past 9, reaching home shortly before 10 o'clock. Mr. W. H. Gleave, Lovely- lane, was the secretary for this trip. The workmen connected with Mr. Houghton's Sankey Wire Mills went; to the number of 1,020, by two trains, leaving Bank Quay Station, at 6.38 and 6.43 a.m., to Blackpool, which place they reached about a quarter to 9. There was a great deal of rain there till about noon, and afterwards this subsided and gave place to a strong wind, which dried the grass and enabled the numerous bowlers among the workmen to divert themselves with their favourite game. They left about half-past eight reaching Warrington at a quarter to 11.

div.head: LIMM.
div.p: LIMM.

TIM CHURCH BFLLS.—Another delay has occurred in connection with the above. Last week a fire took place at the works of Messrs. Taylor, Loughborough, damag- ing the scaffolding on which the bells were being tuned. Fortunately, the bells escaped with little injury. Their arrival will, however, be delayed for a short time.

°ROAN RECITALS.—During the strike of fustian cut- ters in Lymm, the Congregatfonal Church. has been 'thrown open from 11 to 12 o'clock daily for a recital on the splendid organ, and also for the singing of some of Sankey and Moody's hymns. The cutters are said to be a most decidedly musical class, and the opportunity of indulging in so pleasant a pastime has been availed of by many. _

THE durrEßs' SOCIETY.—This newly-formed society is growing rapidly. There are now about 420 members, 120 of whom have joined since the 22nd June. Owing to the masters not conceding the list price which they put forward, the hands came out on strike on Saturday. The notice demanding the increased list price does not expire in Manchester and Salford until next Tuesday, but already the merchants have acquiesced in the list price with the exception of one or two alterations, which the men have accepted.

div.head: LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: THE LOCAL BOARD.

IThe monthly meeting of this Board took place on Thursday night. There were present Mr. H. Cameron (chairman), Messrs. Harrison, IVhitelegg, Brazen&le, Swallow, Flolt, Thomason, Ridgeway (law clerk),Mullard (clerk), Mort (surveyor), and Severs (gas manager.) OBSTRUCTION AT TIM CROSS.—The Surveyor called attention to the obstructions again taking place at the Cress. There was a 'bus standing there on Saturday, and he had had occasion to serve notice on Mr. Taylor for placing mowing machines. &c., on the space in front of the Cross.—The Chairman : I suppose you have only got \to summon them? The Surveyor : We have to serve notice first, and keep copies of them. Mr. Holt thought they were drawing the thing too fine.—Mr. Brazendale : They were only an hour or two, and they had better let the matter slip over.—Mr. Whitelegg : They are hardly a nuisance.—The Chair- man: You cannot let one come and stop another. I cannot consent to anything of the smt, after the proceed- ings the Board have taken to assert the right of the public to the space at the Cross.—The matter was allowed to drop.

TECHNICAL EDUCATION Acv.—The Law Clerk read a. letter from the clerk of the County Council, acknowledg- ing the receipt of a notice that the Local Board had adopted the Technical Instruction Act, and stating that the committee had not yet issued any regulations in relation thereto.—Mr. Brazenda.le said it was reported that the money that Board voted for technical education would go to the Grammar School, and he strongly ob- jected to that. He thought it had better be stated at once that was not so. He preferred it should go to the school in the village, where the instruction would reach the people it was designed for.—Mr. Holt was of the same opinion.—The Chairman: We can do nothing until the County Council issue their regulations.—Mr. Brazen- dale: We may contradict it.—The Law Clerk: There is nothing to contradict as nothing has been done. GAS. Raroirr.—The Gas Manager reported that during the last month there had been 66,000 cubic feet more gas made than in the corresponding period last year, and only 3 tons 6 cwts. more ceal were used. He had also sold five tons more coke than last year, and paid £43s. Bd. less wages this quarter than in the same period of last year. The make of gas per ton of coal carbonized lastyear was 9,782 feet; this year for the quarter ending June 25th, it was 10,334, being an in- crease per ton of 552 cubic feet. There has been an in- crease of gas on the quater of 274,000 cubic feet. INTERFERING WITH A METER.—The manager reported that Mr. J. B. Taylor had, without giving notice, re- moved his meter,and took it to Manchester to be tested, after which he had refixed it without his knowledge. He had seen the certificate, which stated that it registered 4 degrees too slow, which was one more than the law al- lowed. The meter had not been stamped.—The Law Clerk said that was a serious matter.—Mr. Holt: There is a penalty attached to that ?—The Law Clerk: Forty shillings, I think.—Mr. Holt: It was probably done in ignorance..—Mr. Brazendale : They had no right to re- move it, and they must not allow that sort of thing. If they allowed everyone to go mollicotting about their meters there was no telling where it would end. They must put their foot down at once.—The Law Clerk: Something of the sort occurred before, and I had instructions printed on the demand note, hoping that it would obviate this sort of thing. He would sug- gest that the Board get a written apology. from Mr. Taylor for interfering with the meter and a promise not to touch it again. He would further advise that the gas manager do not repair the nieter.—Mr. Holt said in the letter to Mr. Taylor the clerk should state that the meter must be at once repaired.—The Law Clerk Certainly. LOWERING) THE PRICKOF Gas.—Mr. Holt gave notice to move at the next meeting of the Board that a reduc- tion be made in the prictkof gas consumed for cooking,, heating, and motive power.—Mr. Thomason asked that the committee in the meantime consider the advisability , of reducing gas for lighting purposes by sd. per 1.000. The Chairman said they could not do that with their pre- sent great leakage, and he quite approved of the action of the committee in lowering the price t.') cooking stoves, Szc., as it would reduce the leakage in the daytime.,

The - 1,200 men who struck work on Thursday at Greenock and Port Glasgow shipbuilding yard against a reduction of wages have not returned notwithstand- ing the recommendation of the Executive to do so. The men declare that they will continue the fight without strike money.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRA.TES
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRA.TES

GONE THROUGH A FORTUNE. At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, Henry Ford, a middle-aged man, was charged with having tra- velled by tiain from Lymm to Warrington, an the pre- vious night without having paid his fare. It was said that defendant belonged to Derbyshire, his relatives in that county being well-to-do people. They had, how- ever, turned against him on account of his dissipated habits. It was further said that he had gone through a fortune in a comparatively short time. While his money lasted he had made four trips across the Atlantic. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed. RUNNING AMUCK WITH A CLASP KNIFE. At the magistrates' court, on Monday,Robert Didsdale, a Scotchman, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Fennell-st., on Saturday night. P.C. 18, who proved the case, said the prisoner was running at people with a clasp knife in his hand. Alderman Harrison (to the prisoner) : What were you doing with a knife in your hand P—The prisoner : I suppose I was filling my pipe, but I did not mean any harm.—The constable said the man had no tobacco uponlhim.--The prisoner, who said he was working at the iron bridge at Latchford, was discharged on payment of ss. costs. CHARGE OF CRIMINAL ASSAULT. At the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday before Alderman Harri son,Thom as Clymes,bricksetter's labourer aged 29, of 4, Pilings Court, Dial-street, was brought up on remand, charged with committing a rape about a quarter to two o'clock on Sunday morning last, upon Mary Taylor, wife of Thomas Taylor, licensed hawker, at the lodging-house of Mrs. Bridget Kimbling, 17, Dial-street, mother-in-law of , the prisoner, and Annie Duffy, her assistant, were charged with being accessories after the fact. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle appeared for the prosecution. Mr. Whittle withdrew the charge against Duffy, and called her as a witness ; and on hearing certain evidence Withdrew also the charge against Kimbling. The prisoner was committed to the assizes, Alderman Harrison consenting to accept bail, the prisoner's own recognisances of £2O and two sureties for £lO each.

' A WILD IRISHWOMAN At the Magistrates' Court,on Thursday,Bridget Loftus, an Irishwoman, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Portland-st., on Wedgesday night. A con- stable having proved the case,stating that she was abusing her son, Mr. Isherwood, estate agent, stated that the defendant deliberately broke four large panes of ‘glass which it had cost 10s. to repair, this having been paid by her son. She stood all Wednesday with a brick in her hand while they were beingrepaired, and said as soon as ever the man put them in she would break them again. The woman her son was lodging with was lying in fits all Wednesday afternoon, through the defendant's threatening language to him. She was very violent also both the previous Friday and Saturday and on Sunday morning. The defendant, who said she was annoyed with her son for not leaving the lodging-house and for giving his money to his landlady instead of to herself, was fined ss. and costs. CHARGE OF STEALING MILE. A. BOY WHO PRETENDS TO ABNORMAL VISION./ At the -Warrington Police Court, yesterday, Joseph Toppin, aged 16, was charged with•stealing, on Sunday ' afternoon, May 31st, a quantity of milk, the property of Wm. Thompscn, of the Avenue Farm, Warrington.—The prosecutor stated that his attention was called on the day mentioned to some boys who were surrounding his cow, and one of them, the prisoner, was milking the animal. When they saw him they ran away. When he had the cow milked that night it only gave half the usual quantity of milk. He put the value of the milk stolen at 2d. He could not see very well from where he stood when he saw the boys.—The prisoner said he was ill in bed from influenza at the time, and put in a certi- ficate from Dr. Adams supporting his assertion.—John Craddock, a boy, called for the prosecution, said he saw the prisoner milking ithe cow. He was sure it was he, and there were six boys altogether. On his admitting- that he was as distant from them as he was now froth Market-gate, the Bench immediately dismissed the case. ANOTHER POOR LUNATIC AND HIS TOPOGRAPHY. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Daniel Galvin, was charged with being found wandering in Or- ford-street, on Saturday night, he being of unsound mind. P.C. Bell said he saw the prisoner after tena'clock trying to get over a factory wall. He said he had brother who lived over there in a house of his own. Witness told him he could not very well get that way, and he commenced to be very strange. He told him he belonged to Bradford, and on witness asking him if he knew where he was, he said he was in Brad- ford. He was quite sober.—The prisoner in reply to the Mayor, said he was now in Bradford.—The Mayor: You think you are in Bradford now.—The prisoner: lam not sure. I may be.—The Constable and Inspector Spinks said the man was going about from door to door looking for his uncle.—The prisoner: I was looking for my uncle.—lnspector Spinks said the prisoner in the cells was talking for an hour to somebody he thought was in- side.—The prisoner stated that he was with his uncle on Friday night, and that he had gone to the bad through drink.—He was remanded to the workhouse for in- quiries.

OEFENDERS IN THE PARK. Before the borough magistrates, on Monday, Joseph Beddowes, a young man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the Park on Sunday afternoon.—A Constable deposed to finding him asleep on the grass near the band stand, lie roused him up and when he got up be could hardly stand. Then as he would not go away witness took him into custody.—lnspector Bowen said there were great complaints made about men get- ting drunk and lying down in the park, and children having to pass over them.—The prisoner denied that he was drunk.—The Chief Constable said he thought a man drunk and asleep ought to have been allowed more lati- tude.—The Mayor said some people slept very soundly, and a youth roused suddenly from sleep would have a difficulty in standing straight at first. Mr. Hunt (to the constable) : You gave him no time to go away.—Police- Sergeant Chandley said the prisoner was brought to the bridewell drunk. He was fined 53.---james Henry Ardern, employed at Dallam Forge, was charged with smoking,on Sunday last,in a summer i -house n the Park, contrary to the bye-laws of the borough. Mr. Hunt gave him an excellent previous character, but he was fined 2s. 6d. A SUSPICIOUS CHARACER.—HIS DEFENCE WAS THAT HE

WAS GOUTY. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, Thomas Johnson, an elderly man, was charged with being a per- son of suspicious character, and attempting to pick the pocket of Ellen Monks. Mr. Hunt said the prisoner stated that he was 65 years of age, and that he was from Chester and was on his way to Stockport. He was a hawker of pencils, spectacles, &c. The complainant was the wife of Thos. Monks, plumber, residing in Kendrick- st. On Friday morning, when a number of peopl(4 were standing in Sankey-st., to see the procession, Mrs. Monks among them, she, feeling something drag at her dress pocket, felt in it,but found her purse there. She said to her husband, who was with her, "That man," pre- sumably meaning the prisoner, "has been trying to pick my pocket." Her husband watched the man, and saw him go to two or three other women, and lift his knee up to their pockets as if to ascertain whether there was anything in them. He had on a pair of boots that were cut lengthwise, and Mrs. Monks had identified the prisoner's boots as these. P.C. Critchley had his atten- tion directed to the prisoner's suspicious conduct in

Scotland-road. Mrs. Monks had admitbed that she could not swear to the man. She declined to do so now. Her husband identified him, as also the boots he wore, but could not swear that he saw him do more than Mr. Hunt had stated. The prisoner said he lifted his knees up be- cause they were twitching with gout, which-compelled him to wear cut boots. He was detained ia court for. the arrival of a constable from Chester who was expected to come for a man named Peters charged with neglect of his family there,but as at the close of the court this officer had not presented himself,the Mayor said,though he could be sent to prison for being a suspicious character, as there was no evidence to prove him guilty of any offence he would have the benefit of the doubt and be discharged.

div.head: MINOIt CASES.
div.p: MINOIt CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (chairman), and

Wm. Owen. POCKET-PICKING.—John Murphy, aged 23, a hawker, from Manche.ter, was charged with frequenting Sankey- st. with intent to commit a felony. John Marsh and Thomas Harris, with their wives, were standing at the corner of Arpley-st. watching the procession on Walking Day, when, turning suddenly, Mrs. Harris detected the prisoner's hand in her pocket. As she had lost nothing she made no complaint, but presently saw the prisoner in a suspicious attitude near Mrs. Marsh. On this being mentioned to her she discovered that her purse, contain- ing 55., had been stolen. Herbert Richards of the Park View Temperance Hotel, Sankej-st., proved seeing the prisoner put his hand into Mrs. Marsh's pocket/ He 'had a young man and a young woman with him, apparently his accomplices. He was committed to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.--Thomas Johnson (65), hinter, Ches- ter, was remanded on a charge of attempting to pick pockets. In reply to Mr. Garnett, the Chief Constable said the pockets were at the back—the handiest place possible for pickpockets. Mr. Garnett said they seemed to be placed there on purpose to be picked. The Chief Constable said on Friday he had four reports of women's pockets being picked. OBSTREPEROUS ITALIANS.-LMOVatilli and Cosima Crolla, brothers, were charged with being drunk on Friday at the Central Station. They were Italian organ- grinders who had been playing in Warrington on Walk- ing Day. In the eveninc they went to the Central Station, for the purpose of returning to Manchester, and, according to them, the porters made them play the organs and so miss their train. This so enraged them that they assaulted the porters and they were given info custody.—The Chairman: Do you think the King of Italy would be very much shocked if he came to hear of this, and saw your names in print (Laughter.)—The Bench discharged the defendants on payment of the lock-

up fees. DRUM—Samuel Dagnall, brought up under a warrant on a charge of drunkenness, was fined ss. and costs. WILFUL DAMAGE.—SamueI Parker, a forg.eman, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and refusing to quit the Three Pigeons, and was ordered to pay £2 55., the value of a plate glass window at that house,which he had broken by thrusting his fist through the window. A DESPERATE CHARACTER.—Thomas Blair,Town's-end, who appeared in the dock minus waistcoat and shirt,and with his trousers all tattered and torn, was charged with having on the 16th April used bad language to Thomas Critchley, of the Higher Angel Inn; and with having been drunk on the 18th April at Town's-end.—The prisoner behaved most excitedly in court. He declared that the police had treated him iike a dog. He had been obliged to tear up his clothes to lie upon.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner was a man of the worst possible eHracter, and a most desperate man. The Bench sent the prisoner to gaol for a month with hard labour.—Prisoner: I don't care if you give me ten months. I will not have a month. I appeal to the Sessions, and I will be heard, for the treatment I have been subjected to. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Francomb), _ _ _

, and Alderman Harrison. A SUBJECT FOR THE CHESTER POLICE.—A man named Thomas Peters was brought before theßench, concerning whom it was stated that he was wanted by the Chester Police tor neglect of family. He was ordered to be handed over to the Chester Police accordingly. Danix.—Thomas Carr was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and ref using to quit the Pelican Inn, Buttermarket- st., on Saturday night.—Henry Fogg and James Pickett were charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Theatre Tavern, Scotland-road, and Pickett was charged with doing wilful damage to a glass window at the house, to the extent:of 255. It was stated that Pickett struck Fogg and knocked his head through the window.—Pickett dented that he did the latter, and said Fogg struck him first and he struck back and ,Fogg's head must have gone through the window.—Fogg Was fined 10s. and Pickett 10s. and costs.—Ralph Taylor, drunk and disorderly in Orford-lone on Saturday night,who had struck his father in the street several times, was sent to prison for 14 days. —Martin Nicholls, drunk in Sankey-st., on Saturday night, was fined ss.—George Hopkins, 24th appearance, was charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Stranger's Arms, Dial-st., on Saturday night, and with assaulting a man unknown.—P.C. Amson proved the cases, and said he saw the defendant knock a young man down but he went away and witness could not find who it was.—Hopkins was sent to jail for a month.—Joseph Miller' for being drunk and disorderly in School Brow, on the 20th inst., ss.—Brian Belly in Old-road, Latchford, on the 19th inst., and assaulting his wife on the same date. 10s. and costs.—George Townsend was summoned for being drunk in charge of a horse.—His case was ad- journed-. AN UNLICENSED DOG.—John Moon, labourer at Bewsey Forge, charged with keeping a dog without a license, was fined the costs, 3s. 6d. OBSTRUCTING THE THOROUGHFARE.—Maria Harding was fined the costs, 3s. 6d., for obstructing the thorough- fare by allowing a barrel of potatoes to stand on the foot- way at the corner of Victoria-st., on the 24th of June.— John Walton was ordered to pay costs, 75., for allowing a horse and vehicle to stand in,the Market an unreason- able time on the same date. - -

ToEshay.—Before Alderman Harrison, Mr. E. M. Crosfield, and Mr. R. Garnett. KNOCKING A WIFE ABOUT.—William Bibby was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Town's End on the previous night, and with having assaulted his wife.—P.C. 18, said that he saw the prisoner knocking his wife about like a lump of wood. On the officer inter- fering, Bibby became violent, and attempted to strike him. A fine of 103. and costs was imposed in respect of each charge, or,in default of payment, a month's impri- sonment. "A FRIENDLY EMBRACE."—SamueI Feltham and Isaac Rogers were charged with having been drunk and guilty of fighting with each other on the previous night at Brook-place. One of the defendants said they had a friendly quarrel with each other, and the other said it was nothing but a friendly spar.—Mr. Garnett: Just a friendly embrace or something of that kind. (Laugh- ter.) A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed on each. AN UNPROVOKED ASSAULT.—Joseph Bibby was charged with having assaulted P.C. Cooper on the previous night. It seemed that Cooper had been on duty at Town's- end that night, when .the prisoner came up behind him, and, without saying anything, kicked his legs from under him. The only reason for this unprovoked assault appeared to be that Bibby thought Cooper was the officer who had taken his brother into coustody. There was rather a black record againstprisoner, and he was now sent to gaol for three months' hard labour. ASSAULTING BAILIFFS.—David Peters, an elderly man, was charged with having assaulted William Burrows and Thomas Frain, County Court bailiffs, in the discharge of their duties that morning. It seemed that Burrows and Frain were carrying out an order of the County Court at defendant's house, when defendant .assaulted them. Defendant pleaded guilty, and said his temper had got the better of him. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed. THURSDAY.—Before Captain Ridgway (chairman), and Alderman Sutton. QUITE AT HOME IN ANOTHER'S ElOUSE.—George Knott, a very respectable-looking man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., the previous day at noon. P.C. Mill, who proved the case, said the prisoner went into the house of Mrs. Preston,the butcher, and sat down on the sofa and she had to call witness in to get him out: He was fined ss. and costs, Bs. 6d. in all. FRlDAY.—Before Major Pickmere, and Aldermen Harri- son and Burgess. DRUNK.—John Tighe, labourer, drunk in Bridge-st., the previous afternoon, was fined 55., including costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Joseph Warburton, aged 25, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., on Thursday afternoon, and assaulting his father, John Warburton, on the same occasion. The prisoner had only been out jail a week, where he had been four months for assaulting his father and brother. —The deputy Magistrates' Clerk said there was another summons against the prisoner for Mohday.—The cases were proved by a constable and the prisoner's father,who said his son knocked him down,and said lie would never be easy till he finished him entirely.—Major Pickmere paid the prisoner would be mtirdering somebody some day.—Alderman Harrison said 25 lashes would do the prisoner good.—Major Pickmere : Better write to the Home Secretary—Alderman Harrison: Better write to tohim i allow us to do it. I should be delighted to wit- ness t.—The prisoner was sent to jail for a month for the first offence, and for two months for the sissault, with hard labour in each case; Major Pickmere remark- ing that it was necessary to send him away for the public safety as well as for his own interest. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.— James Wooley, was charged with cruelly treating a horse by ova loading it on:the 20th of June. Inspector Dowty said about 10 p.m. on Satur- day night he saw the defendant driving a waggonette with nine passengers. The hwrse was a poor old animal not fit to be drawing such a load. Witness expostulated with the defendant, and requested him to have some of the passengers out, but he refused to do so. n Witness th went back for a constable, and they followed e defen- dant, who was driving to Sankey, and found that he was now driving eight passengers. Inspector Bowen corroborated the, latter part of this evidence. The defendant called several witnesses, who denied that the horse was overloaded, but he was fined 103., including costs. AssArtas.—Mary Bennett was charged with assaulting Mary Tobin on the 26th of June, and James Tobin, her son, was charged with assaulting Mary Bennett. Both

parties were bound over to keep the peace.—Joseph Car- rington was charged with assaulting Elizabeth Burrows on the 27th of June and was also bound over.—Mary Ford, employed at dockhedge Factory, was charged with assaulting Peter Ford, her brother-in-law, on June 28th. 'I he case .was dismissed.—Peter Appleton was charged with assaulting Margaret Scott in Chorley7st.' on the 29th of June and Margaret Scott with assaultlug Sarah Jane Appleton, the previous defendant's daughter.—Appleton was dismissed, and Scott was bound over to keep the peace. THREATENINO.—Thomas Jackson was charged ny Clara Jackson, his sister-in-law, with assaulting and threaten- ing her, on Sunday last, and George Jackson was charged with threatening Thomas Jackson on the same occasion.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for Clara Jack- son. He reminded the Bench that recently she had sum- moned her husband, Geo. Jackson for non-maintenance, and he then agreed to pay arrears and provide a house for her. Her husband was becoming quite a different man, and the parties were willing to live together. He (Mr. Davies) had then appeared °for Mrs. Jackson, but now appeared for the husband, whose brother seemed to be sorry that he was going back to live with his own wife.—Thomas Jackson accepted the proposal of Mr. Davies that each party should withdraw proceedings, Mr. Davies promising that a condition made by Thomas that he should not be troubled in future should be, ob- served.
WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. P. Stubs (chairman), and
T. Comber.

REFUSING TO QUlT.—William Stone, for being, on June 16th, disorderly on licensed premises.the Pear Tree Inn, Burtouwood, occupied by Richard Taylor, and refusing to quit, was fined 2s. 6d. and C.OSI.S. THEFT OF HALF-A-CllOWN.—Thornas Wetton, a respec- tably-dressed young man, from Manchester, was charged with stealing half-a-crown, from the shop of Mr. Joseph Sohofield, grocer, at Earlestown, of which Mr. Joseph Littler is manager, on the 12th June.—Mr. Littler de- posed tc seeing the prisoner, who was occasionally an as- sistant in the shop, making motions about the cash box, and subsequently found that the half-crown had been abstracted and put into an adjacent drawer. Witness marked the coin, and found some time after that it had disappeared, and it was discovered that the prisoner had stolen it. He admitted the theft, and was fined is. and costs, £1 Bs. 3d. in all.

J. A. MacLaren facing S. M. Crosfield and Harrison. MacLaren opened his account by despatching the Warr- ington captain to the boundary twice in succession. Har- rison opened with a maiden, narrowly missing bowling the chief scorer with his third ball. Some smart fielding got Crankshaw run out, and one wicket was done for 30. Smith relieved Crosfield at this total, but his first ball was productive of seven,the result of an over-throw. Howe opened cautiously,and singles marked his opening scores, whilst, on the other hand, MacLaren hit with vigour' some of his strokes, especially his drives, being fine hits. With the total at 57, he placed one in the hands of cover point,the retiring batsman having made 51. Sowler fell to a good catch by Dun, and Knowles and Rowley caused little trouble. Howe and Penning- ton stayed together whilst 34 runs were added, and Rover, who had relieved Smith, puzzled the homesters with his lobs. With the total at 107 for seven wickets, luncheon was taken. On resuming the innings was brought to a close in 20 minutes for 131 runs, Howe carrying out his bat for a well-played 44. Warrington commenced with E. Roper and J. J. Crosfield, Mold and Irving bowling. With the total at eight Roper played on, but Lee and Crosfield Played remarkably fine cricket. Pennington relieved Irving, but to no purpose, and it was not until the total had reached 52 that Mold bowled the visiting professional with a grand ball. Runs were piled on quickly by S. M. and J. J. Crosfield, and at 75 the latter was caught off Mold. A run later the visiting captain played late at one from the fast bowler. G. Clarke and Smith both reached double figures, but Mold in both instances was credited with a wicket. Voisey put together seven in two hits, while Dun was out first ball. The innings closed for 110, Captain Manson being unable to bat, having severely sprained himself while fielding. Score and bowling analysis :
