Having referred to the necessity of early religious edu- cation, he said he had seen a letter in a newspaper, asking if the Y.M.C.A. might not be thinking too much about the physical department. He quite agreed with physical. social, and educational matters being looked after' but he should likewise be always ready to believe that the Association was carrying out work under the name which it held. Therefore he did hope it would carry out what it professed to be—a Young Men's Chris- tian Association. (Hear, hear, and applause.) A vote of thanks was then accorded to the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. HORDEN, seconded by Mr. KERRY ; and a similar vote was passed to the Mayor and Mr. Davies, on the motion of Mr.JoaNFAIRCLOUGH, seconded by Mr. J. R. Bucrrox. The proceedings then termi- nated, many of those present, however, staying to look through the building. A conversazione was to have been held in the evening on the lawn adjoining the building, a large marquee having been provided for the purpose, but, unfortu- nately, the elements were most unpropitious, and the company which presented itself, had to be content, instead of having a pleasant outdoor meeting, i with being crowded n the somewhat confined lecture room. Councillor Shaw Green presided, and expressed his regret at the disappointment caused to those present through the conversazione having to be held indoors. A special hymn having been sung, prayer was offered up by Mr. W. H. Bailey, a Wesleyan local preacher. The secretary then, for the edification of -those who had not been present in the afternoon, re-read the report. The audience were then favoured with aperformance in good style, by a band under the direction of Mr. J. B. Cald- well. The Chairman followed with an address. He said one feature of the report was exceedingly pleasing to him, and that was, that there was an increase of membership of about 50 per cent. (Applause.) He did not see why this increase should not go on, as in Warrington there were young men enough in all conscience who were spending their evenings aimlessly, and if they would only come and join that association they would meet with a pleas- ant place there to pass their evenings, and good com- panionship. He felt deeply thankful that the association had been able to find such a comfortable home. It was not every place that would have suited them, they were such a large family. He felt convinced that there was sufficient enthusiasm in the meeting to 'enable them to carry on that association to a right noble and glorious success. (Applause.) After another excellent perform- ance by the band, Mr. Garnett gave a recitation "The stowaway," which was much applauded.—Mr. Arm- strong, travelling secretary of the Young Men's Christian Association, gave a history of the foundation of that association in 1844 by young men in the employ of the firm now known as Hitchcock. Williams, and Co., drapers, St. Paul's Churchyard, London. The first meet- ing was held in a bedroom on the draper's premises. A young man who was chairman of a free and easy at a public-house round the corner, was induced to come to this meeting, and was con- verted, and became a prominent Christian worker, and instrumental in starting one of the most powerful Chris- tian organs that existed that day. (Applause.) There were now 609 Y.M.C.A.associations in this country with a membership of 64,640. Throughout the world there were 4,012 associations,with over 350,000 members. The object of the Young Men's Christian Association, the weaker pointed out, was to advance the interests of its members spiritually, intellectually, socially,and physi- cally, and he expressed the hope that the town of War- rington would help the members of the local association to carry out the work they had so well begun. A collec- tion having been made, there was another performance by the band, after which the conversazione concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman,to Mr. Armstrong and others. Subsequently refreshments were partaken of by the members of the association and by a :number of ladies who were present, by the former in the reading loom and by the latter in the parlour. We are requested to mention that a telegram was received from Mr. Jame- son, of Liverpool, district secretary, regretting the fact of his inability to attend.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

*** Secretaries of Cricket Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

Sr. PAUL'S CHURCH CHOIR V. THE THIRD CLASS OF THE SAME ScnooL.—Score :—St. Paul's Choir, 49; The Third Class of the Same School, 48. Sr. MARTS V Sr. ALBANS.—This match was played on Walking Day, and resulted in a win for St. Mary's. Score :—St. Mary's 34; St. Albans 15. CADISHEAD V. IRLAM CRICKET CLUE.—The match be- tween the above cluband Patricroft excited considerable interest in the village, being the first meeting of the clubs this season. The morning was very wet, but about three o'clock in the afternoon the rain ceased, leaving a strong south-west wind blowing. Patricroft went in first, and entrusted the defence to Anderton and Abbott, who faced the bowling of Austwick and Arstall. Neither of the batsmen seemed at ease with the bowling, and after ten minutes' play the partnership ceased, having yielded nine runs. Bad luck followed, three men being run out, and the innings finally terminated for 31 runs. Cadis- hEad sent in Aostwick and Yarwood, who faced the bowl- ing of Rogers and Abbott. Yarwood made three and then was run out. Matters, however, mended, Austwick making 13 before being caught, and Dr. Jago 15. Upon L. Taylor and C. Brooks becoming partners matters be- came lively, and continued so until Brooks was bowled for 13. Upon R. B. Toft joining L. Taylor the two played time out, L. Taylor having made 21, most of which were singles. The score for seven wickets was 82 runs, this being an easy win for Cadiskead by 51 runs.

WARRINGTON V. LIVERPOOL.—The first meeting OA these clubs this season tofik place on Saturday, at Arpley. The chances of Warrington inflicting defeat were ceitainly at a very, low ebb when it was found that such players as S. M. Crosfield, :Captain Manson, and Captain Adam were absent, whilst, on the other hand, Liverpool placed an exceptionally strong team in the field. To mend matters, Warrington were unfortu- nate in losing the toss, an advantage which certainly decided the fortunes of the day. H. B. Steel and Parr were the first to take up the defence, R. Smith and J. J. Crosfield being the bowlers. The former's first over was productive of a couple, but the first ball from J. J. bowled Steel's middle stump. Another run only had been added when Smith bowled F. C. Pilkington, whilst in his following over he also dismissed Parr, the tele- graph board showing the state of the game to be 6-3-5. With D. Q. Steel and the Rev. Mr. Brutton as partners a slight stand was made, but only 13 runs had been added since the last wicket fell when Brutton was bowled. Melly was well caught by Dutton without any score attached to his name, so that half the wickets were down for 25 runs, Crosfield up to this time having secured 3 wickets for 11 runs. An agreeable change came over the game for Liverpool when E. C. Hornby joined his captain. Runs came freely on one occasion Hornby putting in a splendid drive over the flag staff, the ball going clean out of the ground. L. Smith relieved his brother at 44, but the change did not act, two overs sufficing for his brother again to take up the attack. Harrison checked the run,getting a trifle,and after he had sent down four over he crossed to Smith's end, Crosfield resuming at his old place. Harrison with an extra quick one dismissed Steel at 86, the partnership having realized 61 runs, the out-going batsman share being 52, in which were seven fours. With only another run added Stephens was bowled, and then H. C. Pilkington and Hornby made another useful stand. As a last resource Dutton was given a trial, and strange to say, the innings was soon brought to a close, for after Horn- by had been bowled for a capital 38, Pilkington and Gregory were dismissed with successive balls, the total having reached 111. Warrington commenced the diffi- cult task of obtaining the runs at 5 o'clock, and the open- ing batsmen were Smith and Crosfield. A promising start was made, as 26 runs were notched before White- head bowled Smith with a good ball. The bowlers had a great advantage on the fast drying wicket. and White- head got a great amount of work on the ball. Lee and Crosfield took the score to 39, when Whitehead, with a ball that broke fully a foot from the off, dismissed the home captain. Lee was. unfoOunately caught off his hand by D. Q. Steele standing far behind the wicket, and G. Clarke being tempted to hit Out at Whitehead missed and paid the penalty. With 39 runs on the board, the prospects of Warrington winning were indeed but slight, and the remaining batsmen being apparently beaten before they reached the crease, only 13 runs were added, of which Voisey made eight, and the innings closed for 52 runs Liverpool winning by 59. WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER.—This return match took place at Old Trafford on Monday. Fine cricket weather prevailed, but there was but a poor attendance when play was commenced at 12.40. The first match re- sulted in a victory for our local team by 19 runs, and Manchester were evidently bent on reversing this verdict, for besides having the assistance of several prominent amateurs, the services of Mold, the Lancashire bowler, werealso requisitioned. Warrington's ill-luck was again with them, Manchester electing to bat, Crankshaw and

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.

TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman), Jame Marson, W. C. Jones, H. Neald, and W. Long. ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF Cows.—Charles Harold Broad- bent, of Latchford, for illegally removing, on the 14th of April, a cow from the sheduled district, Latchford, to Walton, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.—John Fairclough, J.P., and Samuel Williams, both of Latchford, for illegally removing cows from Latchford to Acton Grange, on the 3rd of June, were fined 2s. 6d. and costs each. ADULTERATING COFFEE.—Thomas Dutton, provision dealer, Higher Whitley, for selling to Inspector Roger Hind, coffee adulterated with 25 per cent, chicory, was fined ss. and costs. A WALTON INNKEEPER AND HIS CUSTOMERS.—Thomas Smith, navvy, James Morris, navvy, and William Wimperley, labourer, all of Walton, were charged with being found drunk, on the 4th of June, on the licensed premises of William Beswick, the Ship Inn, Walton ; and William Beswick was charged with permit- ting them to be drunk on his premises on the occasion.— Mr. A. Browne. solicitor, of Warrington, appeared on behalf of the county police, for the prosecutor, and Mr. It. Davies, solicitor, of Warrington, for the defence. Evi- dence was given by Police-Sergeant Booth and P.C: Shatwell, according to which Smith came out of the house drunk, staggering, and holding on to the wall,and Morris and Wimperley were drunk in the house. The Sergeant cautioned the landlord's daughter, who had charge of it, not to supply more to them, and told her to order then% out, but all three netn were subsequently found there drunk. The daughter had told them on the first call they had two pints, and on the second visit the landlord said they had three. The defence was that the men had gone in for shelter from the rain and had some beer while their clothes were drying,and that Smith was lame and could not walk without a stick,hence his holding to the wall, but that they were not drunk, and that the landlord had never been told they were. Smith, Morris, and Wimperley, Were fined 10s. each, including costs,and Beswick was fined 20s. and costs. NOT HAVING HORSES IN CONTROL.—JOSeph Monks and John Pemberton, of Warrington, for being asleep in charge of horses drawing lorries were fined is. and costs each, and James Hartley for being too distant from his horse and cart, was fined 25. 6d. and costs. FIGHTING.—James Shepherd, shopkeeper of Lymm, charged with fighting at Grappenhall,on the 28th of May, was dismissed. DRUNK.—John Grounds, labourer, of Walton, drunk on the 6th of June, at Walton Superior' was fined ss. , DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—WaIter Goodman, drunk and disorderly at Stockton Heath, orrthe 6th of June, John Maire, blacksmith, at Grappenhall, on the 14th of June, Alfred Stringer, labourer, of Acton Grange, at Walton Superior, on June 15th, and John Rustage, labourer, of Acton Grange, at Stockton Heath, were each fined 2s. ed. and costs. A LEGH PUBLICAN'S AND HIS WIFE'S EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT.—Thomas Bower, landlord of the Bridge Inn, Little Legh, was charged that on the 30th of May he was found drunk on his own licensed premises; he was also charged with being found drunk there on June 18th. Ellen Bower, his wife, was charged with being found drunk there on the 30th of May, with being drunk on the highway on the 10th of June, and also with being drunk on her husband's premises, on the 12th ot June. They pleaded not guilty in each case. Mr. Browne, appeared, for the prosecution. Police-Sergeant Dutton said on May 30th he went to the Bridge Inn,accompanied by P.C. Richardson, and saw Mrs. Bower in the bar very drunk. He could not find Mr. Bower, and came out, but on account of what he heard went in again and found him asleep on the sofa, his servant girl trying to wake him. Shortly afterwards the servant came and said she was looking for Mr. Bower and she could not find him. Witness found him lying in the hayloft, and got him into the house. Mrs. Bower commenced to be very dis- orderly again, and he put her into the house three times, and he told Mr. Bower to try to lock her in, but he told witness to take her and lock her up,calling her by a profane name, and saying he could do no good with her. On the 10th of June she Was drunk on the high- way, and broke several panes of glass. The way she and her husband had been carrying on was scandalous. —Mr. Bower said on the 30th of May he was lying on 1 the sofa because he was suffering from influenza.—Mr. ' Browne: People suffering from influenza don't go into a hayloft.—P.C. Richardson corroborated the sergeant's statement.—P.C. Gibbon also deposed as to instances in which the defendants had been drunk.—Annie Clark said she had been a servant at the house nine wereks,and 1 the defendants were drunk on June 10th. On the latter date she banged witness out without reason. She was off and on drunk all the time witness was employed there. —The Bench had a private consultation, and fined Mr. Bower 10s. and costs for the first offence, the second was withdrawn on payment of costs, and Mrs. Bo wer was fined 10s. and costs in the first case, and the other cases against her were withdrawn on payment of costs. • DOGS AT LARGE UNMUZZLED.—John Groves, of Latch- ford, for having two dogs at large unmuzzled, at Grap- penhall, on the 25th of May, was fined 2s. and costs. THE CHARGE OF B4ER-STEALING AT ANT ROBUS . Joseph Monks, Christofoher Barlow, and Charles Sit- gram, all of Warrington, were brought up on remand from the Occasional Court, charged with stealing 'beer, on the 23rd of June, the property of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., brewers. Evidence was given by 1 P.C.'s Mellor and Evans from which it appeared that the' following were the facts. The prisoners were in charge of three lurries, on which they were conveying barrels of beer from Wilderspool to Northwich. The police, who had had complaints from their employers about beer being stolen from their lurries. The constables accord- ingly secretly followed the prisoners on the day in ques- tion. On reaching a quiet spot in the high road at Antrobus they drew up the lurriesin such a position that no one could see from the highway what took place, and while Monks went behind the hedge to see if anybody was about, Barlow and Silgram drew the bung of a barrel, and poured some of the contents into a bucket. On Monks coming back the three men proceeded to drink the beer, the police not having been seen. They had secreted themselves, however, and observed all the proceedings; and they then made their appearance, and apprehended the prisoners; who could not deny their guilt. The prisoners were now fined 103. and costs each.

div.head: RETIREMENT OF CAPTAIN SHAW.
div.p: RETIREMENT OF CAPTAIN SHAW.

Captain Eyre Massey Shaw, C. 8., who has held the position of Chief Officer of the Metropolitan Fire Brigade since the death of Mr. Braidwood, thirty-one years ago, has decided to retire, and has placed his resignation in the hands of the Fire Brigade Committee of the London County Council. The news has been received with much regret by the officers and men of the brigade.

div.head: -op-- THE CMOW CONTEST.
div.p: -op-- THE CMOW CONTEST.

The election campaign in County Carlow entered on 9, distinct phase on Sunday with the arrival of Mr. Parnell, who received addresses in the Town Hall, and also ad- dressed an outside meeting in the town square. The honourable member did. not travel over any new ground, but again dealt with land purchase. The deputation from Tullow was stoned when approaching Carlow, a poor-law guardian and a driver being struck. Mr. Healy addressed an anti-Parnellite meeting at Tullow, and re- ferred in strong terms to Mr. Parnell.—Both parties at Carlow have had organized tours of the constituencies. Mr. Parnell and his supporters proceeded to Leighton Bridge on Monday morning, and the anti-Parnellites proceeded thither later in the day. There was no excite- ment. The nomination of candidates for the Parliamentary vacancy at Carlow,caused by the death of The O'Gorman Mahon, took place on Wednesday, the candidates being Mr. Kettle (Parnellite),and Mr. Hammond (Anti-Farnel- lite). The polling takes place on the 7th inst.
WARRINGTON YOUNG MEN'S CHRIS-
TIAN ASSOCIATION.
OPENING OF NEW PREMISES.

The new and very much larger premises of the Warrington Y.M.C.A., at Friar's Green, were, on Wednesday, opened by Mr. J. C. Parr, the president of the Association. The new abode of the Associa- tion is the large house recently occupied by Mrs. Bowes, and it is in several ways excellently adapted for the purposes to which it is now to be put. There will be a large lecture room, a reading room and rooms to be used as class rooms. There will also be accommodation for the caretakers, Mr. and Mrs. Yeadon, and three bedrooms will be furnished. In addition, there is a large-sized garden and lawn, which will, it is obvious, be useful acquisitions. The interior of the building has been tastefully decor- ated by Mr. W. Winstanley, of Park-place. The membership of the Association is now 170, thus showing an increase of about fifty per cent. upon the membership *roll as it stood when the Associa- tion entered upon the new premises a fort- night or three weeks ago. At the time of the formal opening of the building, on Wednesday afternoon, there was a fair attendance, including Mr. J. C. Parr who occupied the chair, the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), Mr. Joseph Davies, Rev. F. Lake Good, Mr. J. It. Buckton, Councillor Jenkins, Mr. M. Milling, Mr. R. Garnett, Councillor James Fairclough, Mr. C. H. Kerry, Mr. J. S. Garland, Mr. John Fairclough, Mr. H. Horden, Mr. R. E. Garnett, (treasurer), Mr. T. Wallington (secretary), Rev. H. V. Pigott, Mr. Clay, Mr. Wyllie (chairman of the Committee), Mr. J. T. Pattison (financial secretary), Mr. H. Armstrong (travelling secretary), and Mr. Hesketh. The proceedings were opened with the singing of a hymn and the offering up of a prayer by the Rev. 11. V. Pigot. The secretary (Mr. Wall- ington) mentioned that he had received apologies for non-attendance from Mrs. S. Reynolds, M. and Mrs. J. Lyon Whittle Rev. J. Yonge, Mr. Jeans, Mr. Newett, (secretary Of the Manchester Y.M.C.A.), Mr. Lightfoot (secretary of the St. IlelensY.M.C.A.), and Mr. Z. Armitage, J.P. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said he must begin by congratulating the Association upon the premises in which they found themselves that day. He was sure a great deal of taste had been displayed in the remodelling of the premises' and he felt sure, from what he had been able to see, that they would serve the purposes of the Association and improve its prospects in every way. (Hear, hear.) There were many thoughts that would occur to them that day. They would remember that a few years ago the Associotion was very weak and very insignificant, and domiciled in a very indifferent way, and even perfectly inadequate to their then very modest requirements. But energy, patience, and perseverance had succeeded, as he thought he might say they almost always did succeed when the cause was a good one, and when the requirements were reasonable. (Hear, hear.) Those who originated that movement in Warrington had, by their discretion, their tact, and their moderation, secured the sympathies and the well-wishes of those of their friends and neighbours —and he was glad to say there were many of them—to whom the care and the welf3re of youth was not only a duty but a privilege. (Hear, hear.) He felt tha t those who led and those who followed might all be excused a little pardonable pride that day when they Caine to the inauguration of their new departure. (Hear, hear, and applause.) But, although their first thoughts must be those ef thankfulness for the providence which had pros- pered them so far, he thought their next thoughts must be those of anxiety that the good beginning they had made should be continued, and that no success should induce them to depart from the care and caution so neces- sary to their Association. (Hear, hear, and applause.) While, as he felt sure they should, they went from strength to strength and increasing in numbers and in power, he hoped they should not forget to cultivate that modesty and that deference to the opinions of others, which was always so becoming in youth, and that they should avoid giving or taking offence as far as theycould conformably with their duty to the Association and them- selves. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Parr then addressed some words of advice to the younger members of the Associa- tion, and concluded by declaring the building open. The SECRETARY (Mr. T. Wallington) then submitted his report. He said that on that occasion he felt extremely proud that he was in a position to announce to them that, after anxiously waiting for a considerable period, and after doing all in their power for the good of the members, and fighting against all the difficulties met with in the old premises in Bold-st., the Committee had ventured to rent the premises they were publicly open- ing that day, which were admirably suited for the more extensive work which had been contetnplated so long. It was the intention of the Committee to commence classes of various descriptions as early as possible, and they earnestly appealed to all the members to at once speak out and state what subjects they would specially , desire to study, as they felt that without this expression of feeling on the part of the members to guide them, all their efforts in the direction of educational enterprises would be futile. It was the wish of the Committee to make the spiritual welfare of the young men who threw in their lot with them a predominant feature in the working of the Association. (Hear, hear.) He was proud to state that since they had taken over those pre- mises the membership had increased about 50 per cent., and this had greatly encouraged the Committee and stimulated them to greater exertions. (Applause.) The TREASURER (Mr. R. E. Garnett), in a report, said they estimated that the cost of furnishing, done in the most economical way, would be about £250 and against that they had now £195, a sum which included a gift of £lOO from the President. (Applause). The honorary subscriptions amounted to something like £3O, and their members' subscriptions to £2O, but as they had had an increase of members this last sum would be in- creased also. Their estimated annual expenditure would be about £155, and if they could raise the membership to between 300 and 400 with subscriptions amounting to £75, while the honorary subscribers gave £lOO, they should feel the association stood on a firm footing. The MAYOR, in a short address, spoke in favour of providing amusements for the younger people, and also in commendation of the intention to have classes. He thought Warrington had some of the best elementary schools in the country, yet as soon as children left those schools they had no means of learning French or German or making themselves useful for commercial pursuits. He thought if they could but get qualified teachers of French and German that would be very useful know- ledge to add to the many other useful things taught in that institution. Mr. H. ARMSTRONG (travelling secretary) next gave an address as to the general objects of the Young Men's Christian Association, and also the very large number of these institutions now existing. Mr. Jos. DAVIES next gave an address. He mentioned that that new home of the Association was built by a worthy banker, Mr. Turner, in the early part of this century ; and he added, that he had received the earliest rudiments of his education in thathouse. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: DOUBLE BIGAMIST.
div.p: A DOUBLE BIGAMIST.

At the Old Bailey, on Thursday, Henry Fison Bur- gess, 49, baker, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude on charges of committing bigamy and stealing large sums of money. Taking advantage of his wife's absence abroad, the prisoner married first Rachael Gill, domestic servant, of Bristol, and ;subsequently Miss Snooks, another servant; obtaining a considerable sum from each.

div.head: TERRIBLE TORNADO IN GERMANY.
div.p: TERRIBLE TORNADO IN GERMANY.
SEVERAL KILLED AND INJURED.

CREFELD, TIIITIISDAY.—A terrible tornado has swept over this district carrying away the hall and booths erected on the ground of the Rhenish Federal Riflemen now assembled here for practice, and destroying about 50 houses between Suechteln, Viersen, and Duelken. Several persons have been killed and injured.
THE GERMAN EMPEROR'S VISIT TO
ENGLAND.

By the Queen's command, the German Emperor and Empress will be met at Port Victoria, to-day (Saturday), by the Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke of Connaught, and the Duke of Clarence and Avondale. The Prince and Princess of Wales, with the Princesses Victoria and Maud of Wales, will await their majesties at the South-West- ern Railway Station at Windsor, and accompany their majesties to the grand entrance to the Castle, where they will be received by the Queen. Arrangements are being made by the naval authorities at Sheerness for the reception of the German Emperor and Empress on Saturday afternoon. The Imperial yacht Hohenzollern, escorted by a German squadron, is ex- pected to arrive at the Nore about one o'clock. It has now been arranged that at the conclusion of the Emperor's official visit, his Majesty will cruise for a fort- night round the Scottish coast in his yacht, the Meteor, and will eventually compete for the Queen's Cup in the Royal Yacht Squadron Regatta at Cowes. The Empress and the Crown Prince will remain at Windsor until the close of the official visit, and will then travel to Ports- mouth, embarking en the Royal yacht Alberta for con- veyance to Norris Castle, which has been placed at her Majesty's disposal by the Duchess of Bedford. Here the Empress will be joined by the remainder of her family, and will remain until after the Cowes week, when the whole of the German Imperialtfamily will return iu the Hohenzollern.
ATHLETIC SPORTS AT ST. HELENS.

The first amateur athletic festival in connection with the St. Helens Rugby Football Club com- menced on the ground of the club in Knowsley-rd., St. Helens, on Friday night. There was a fairly large attendance of spectators, considering the in- clement weather at the time announced for the start. The judges were Messrs.J. Higson (Salford), F. T. Parry, It. Wilcock (Liverpool), J. W. Davies (Widnes), R. Tipping and It. Seddon (St. Helens) ; referee and timekeeper, Mr. J. J. Tickle; starter, Mr. J. M‘Manus ; treasurer Mr. John Tyrer, and secretary Mr. F. The results of the various events were as follow :-300 Yards Boys Race : 1, Charles Gould (Sutton),so yards; 2, Fred' Burgess (Widnes), 60; 3, Joseph Valentine (St. Helens), 30; time, 384 secs. 220 Yards Flat Race: 1, T. CRICKET.

Lancashire has suffered another defeat, this time at the hands of Nottingham. The play during the whole of the three days was emphatically shw, and the Nottingham publicatayed away in great numbers. The Lancashire men began very badly, and scarcely seemed to recover from the shock of Barlow's loss :from the first ball of the match and had it not been for the batting of Mr. Cros- field and some of the members of the " tail " the first innings would have been a disastrous failure. In the second innings the batting improved somewhat, and Baker's 40 was a most valuable contribution; but Notts seemed to have the upper hand all through, and the 123 runs required were hit off for the loss of three wickets-- all taken by Briggs.

On the winning side, Shrewsbury again failed to d& himself the least justice. He has played six or seven innings, and his aggregate does not amount to 50 runs certainly an unprecedented record of his career. Albert Ward also failed in both innings. In practice and in club matches, as he showed against the Manchester Club and Ground on Wednesday, he can hit with great vigour; but when opposed to first-class bowling he becomes timid. In physique he is the ideal cricketer; and if he could infuse a little more animation into his style, and avail himself a little more of his " length and strength," he would improve his own position and that of his adopted county. He is at present permitting his county-man Baker to eclipse him completely.

Lancashire has nowlost three county matches,won one, and drawn another. Our solitarv;victory was over York- shire. The" in and out" playing. of the so-called first- class counties has been remarkable. Notts has beaten Lancashire and Yorkshire, and been, in its turn,defeated by Middlesex and Surrey; and Yorkshire has been beaten by Lancashire, after having defeated Middlesex. The only thing that is clear in the present contest for the championship is that Surrey occupies an absolutely commanding position, and seems likely to come in as easy first.

Abel retains his lead as top batsman of the year with 38.91, and another Surrey man, M. Read, has crept uP to second place by his fine score against Yorkshire earl,' in the week. Martin's bowling average still keeps up, and next to him comes J. T. Hearne, the young Middle- sex professional. W. Attewell has sent down 145 more overs than anybody else, but Lohmann has taken seveli more wickets.

POLISH COLONY AT ST. HELENS.

• The magistrates at the Town Hall were occupied ,a considerable time on Monday afternoon in hearing the case of assault brought by John Ravensburg, a Russian Pole,residing in Chancery-lane.Parr,against Antonio Brazewise, another Pole, of Park-road, and 'three Englishmen, named Harry Watkinson, Peter liankinson. and Peter Highcock, all of Chancery- lane. Mr. J. O. Swift appeared for the defendants. A difficulty arose in the interpretation of the evidence, it being stated that the complainant had brought an inter- peter from Liverpool.—The Clerk (Mr. Davison) said e practice was to get an independent interpreter, and not one selected by one of the interested parties. He k e d if Mr. Swift had an objection to the interpreter— Swift said he had not.—The interpreter gave his name as Mr. Parff, of Liverpool, and said he had acted as 11,1terpreter at Seacomb, and sometimes in the courts at iverpool. According to the evidence of the 'complain- ?k.!tt as interpreted by Mr. Parff, the defendant entered als house and asked for drink. He refused to give them atr, Whereupon they assaulted hitt'. The defence was e denial of the alleged offence, and it was stated that complainant had said, "Me no like English ways,but can use knives."—Mr. Swift remarked that one thing had !!.tonished him was that they should have had a colony °l.l'nles living in Parr for two years and never have heard ot it before, because ever since the Poles landed at Wid- .lles the courts had never been free from them, and nyrYers had had a rich harvest. The only other thing rout which he was astonished was that there should 'ave been such a big fight and so little harm done. The case was ultimately dismissed.

div.head: HEAVY FINES ON FISH SELLERS.
div.p: HEAVY FINES ON FISH SELLERS.

A WARNING AGAINST SELLIrG PUTRID FISH. On Tuesday morning the Warrington magistrates dlalt with a number of charges against fish dealers, and in two instances imposed rather exemplary fines. The town clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) pro. secuted in all the cases. The first case heard was one in which George Bromley, of Liverpool, was charged with having for sale, at Warrington mar- ket, on the 20th of June, 3801bs. of haddock and Sibs. of kipper herring which were not fit for food. Defendant pleaded guilty, but said that when he bought the fish in Liverpool market on the morning of the 20th it seemed perfectly sound. It was also added that the fish had not been taken from the vehicle on which it was carried to the mar- ket, and had not been offered for sale before being seized. Mr. Whittle said the defendant was liable to a fine of £2O in respect of each fish,or to a total amount of £7,360. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed.—Anthony Shield, a young man belonging to St. Helens, was charged with exposing for sale 1111bs of putrid herring. In this case it was stated that the fish was very bad, anti the Town Clerk asked for a substantial penalty. He incidentally remarked that the decision of the magistrates some time ago, to send a butcher to prison for two months for sell- ing stinkinc, meat, had had a salutary effect for a long time. The otal fine to which this defendant rendered himself liable was £10,360. Inspector Norman and Dr. Gornall, the medical officer of health, gave evidence, and, in reply to a question, Dr. Gornall said tbat de- composed fish was a most violent poison. Inspector Norman also added that scarcely a Sunday went past but people brought some bad fish to his house to show how they had been duped. A fine of £5 and costs, in all a 2s. 6d. was imposed, or in default one month's im- prisonment.—Anne Hall and Henry Nixon, of St. Helens. were also charged with offences in connection with sell- ing putrid fish in Warrington market on the 10th June, Hall with selling the fish, and Nixon with causing it to be sold. In this case the fish that had been seized and condemned included cat-fish, haddocks, fluke, grayling, &c., weighing in all 935 lbs, the defendants having laid themselves open to a possible fine of £260,000. The fish was all described as being in a very bad condition. The charge was not pressed severely against Hall, but the Bench was not asked to ,impose a substantial penalty on Nixon. Hall was fined 103. and costs, and Nixon £lO and costs,or, in default, twq months' imprisonment.

At Leeds, on Tuesday, Waltnr Lewis Turner and Ann, his mother, were again charged with being implicated in the murder of Barbara Whitam Waterhouse, a girl aged 6 years, as already reported. On the application of Mr. Catterall, prosecuting solicitor, in which Mr. Willey,the prisoner's solicitor, concurred, both were remanded till Monday next at ten o'clock.
LORD R. CHURCHILL BURNT IN EFFIGY.

A DISAGREEABLE TRAVELLING COMPANION. In the account of his voyage out to the Cape, Lord Randolph Churchill has not a good word to say for any- body connected with the Grantully Castle. Captain, officers, crew, cook—all seem to have been incapable of pleasing him. We (" Pall Mall Gazette ") regret to learn that the dislike was not confined to one side. Indeed, a passenger by the vessel on its return to London assures us that it will be long ere Lord Randolph Churchill and his party are forgotten. "They managed," says our inform- ant, to set everybody on board against them." If all that our informant tells us be true, it is not difficult to under- stand the disfavour with which Lord Randolph's fellow- passengers regarded him. He refused, it seems, to take his place at the general table, and ,bad a separate table arranged in the saloon for himself and his friends. This is one point not altogether expected in one who professes to be a democrat. He sent stewards to request ladies to move from positions they had taken up so that his card-table might be placed conveniently for himself. On Sundays, however, he defied, in a needlessly aggressive manner' the feelings of thp Sabbatarians. From all this it is not surprising to learn that when the vessel arrived at Natal Lord Randolph was burnt in effigy! Lord Randolph's severest criticisms the other day were bes- towed on the food of the Castle line. Some light is perhaps thrown on these criticisms by the indignation which one of Lord Randolph's travelling companions is said to have expressed because some prunes which were served for dinner were not stoned. It was a subject of' no little amusement on board .the Grantully Castle to speculate how a party which objected even to stones in their plums would enjoy roughing it in Mashonoland— an expedition which is not exactly adopted to those who require, as the phrase is, "their rose leaves curled."

THE WARRINGTON EXAMINER SAYS : " THE MARMALADE TRADE.—The severe" " weather we have recently experienced in" "this quarter has extended as tar south as' "Seville. It is in the neighbourhood of" "Seville, that the oranges best suited for " "marmalade making are grewn. A recent" "frost (the like of which has not been ex-" " perienced forten years). hasolayed havoc" "with the fruit, and, although though the" "full extent of the damage is not yet" • known, it is believed that fully one half " "the orange crop has been destroyed." Letter c,' to the Zittor.
THE BANDS ON WALKING DAY.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me space in your valuable paper to say how pleased I was at seeing our bands turn out on Walking Day. I think the Warrington people ought to feel proud of their bands. I should like, with your permission, to Say how proud I felt at seeing theea League of the Cross Brass Band. I think the Catholics might say they have got a band anybody may be proud of, thanks to Mr. Mullins for his conductorship in bringing the band to the front, despite the members that have left.—Yours &c. Warrington, June 30th, 1891.
A LOVER OF MUSIC.
WARRINGTON Y.M.C.A.

Sir,—As Mr. Wallington's letter is rather misleading, and calculated to convey a wrong impression, I may say in reply thereto, that the question for the decision of the Committee at their last meeting was" whether they would allow the evangelistic services to be continued as heretofore when the new premises were opened" and I was led to understand unmistakably that they would not. A suggestion was made that a service might be commenced later in the year, but I maintain it would not be evangelistic, because' it would be exclusively limited to those connected with the Association. I was therefore perfectly correct in stating that the evangelistic services have been discontinued, as the exclusion of strangers would be inconsistent with the term " evange- It seems to me that unless the Committee more clear- ly realise the importance of extending their Christian work beyond the ordinary members, as promoted by kindred Associations, they will not meet with much success. Such healthy games as cricket, lawn-tennis, Sic., are to be encouraged, but the Association should not altogether overlook the praiseworthy object of winn- ing souls to Christ in the summer months as,wen as in winter. I am, Sir, yours faithfully, JOHN ED. HISLOP. 79, Manchester-road, Warrington, July 2nd, 1891.

div.head: THEATRE FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: A THEATRE FOR WARRINGTON.

Sir,—About 12 months ago a report was circulated round the town that Warrington was at last to have A place of entertainment worthy of being called a theatre, but we have not yet seen any steps taken in this direc- tion. My idea in writing to you, sir, is that, if the sub- ject was well ventilated in your columns, it night cause some little spirit to be infused into theatrical life in our town. At present, we have three places of amusement, one a music hall and the other two are supposed to be theatres. How they answer their purpose the people of Warrington are well able to testify. The average enter- tainment provided at these "theatres "is not satisfactory. Occasionally, say, every six months or so, the manage- ment exerts itself and gives us a company like the one that has been performing at the Hall for the past few weeks, and even this otherwise very good performance is spoilt by the very scant amount of orchestra, which con- sists or consisted of one gentleman officiating at a piano. It wosld scarcely be fair.to criticise the music, as, how- ever able a player the gentlemaii might be, it is but poor compensation for an orchestra. Why is Warrington so far behind other towns? Why should we not have at least one large and well-managed , house? Why should the inhabitants of our good old ' town be compelled either to do without, or go either to ' Liverpool or Manchester for an evening's amusement, thus taking their money out of the town. I feel assured that were such an establishment commenced here it wouldbe well patronised, as any one can see by the sup- port which is extended to the hall when (rare event) an opera visits us. There are thousands of people in War- rington who would go regularly to the playhouse (if there was not such a tremendous obstacle in the way as the 2s. 6d. or 2s. 3d. for railway fare, which ever it might be, to say nothing of the lateness of the hour when you arrive home), who never go now from one year's end to the other, because of the average class of entertainment provided for them. Hoping that some enterprising men will see their way to raise the level of theatrical entertainment in War - rington,—l remain, sir, yours truly, " THESPIAN."

div.head: DOCTORS DIFFER.
div.p: DOCTORS DIFFER.

Sir,—At a recent Confirmation by Bishop Jayne at St. John's Dukinfield, he is reported as saying :—" Ile was there that evening as God's appointed messenger and ambassador to bring to them a gift; to bring to them the best of all gifts—the gift of God's Holy Spirit. They had entered the door as infants for Baptism, and passed up the nave, and that day got to the chancel'steps and they were invited now to go further still to the holy altar. The Baptist knew why he was a Baptist. They (the Church of England) did not alone constitute the Church of Christ. They ought always to have a reason why they were members of the Church of England. By private prayer, by the right use of His holy day, by studying their Bibles, and reading them by the light and guidance of their prayer book then they would be fitted to go up to the holy altar of the Lord and become communicants—to join in the highest act of christian worship"—l deny that the Bishop has the power of bringing the gift referred te. The Bible teaches each person to ask for it for him or herself. People are not admitted in Christ's church at infant baptism). Dr. IlicNeile in his famous book the Church and the Churches

writes—the Word of God is silent on infant baptimkk% Dr. J. B. Lightfoot, late Bishop of Durham, in his 'eSm- mentary on Colossians, says—" It is the baptism of believers by immersion." Are infants believers ? Bishop Burnet, in Artick. 27 writes, "Teaching must go before baptism." Dr. R. P. Blakeney writes—" Confirmation is an ecclesiastical rite of the church not instituted by , Christ or his Apostles, and the Prayer Book is but a human compilition." Richard Mant, D.D., Bishop ef Donn, wrote—" Confirmation was not ordained hy Christ." James Begg, D.D., in his hand-hook on Popery writes, "Confirmation was never instituted, by Christ or his Apostles." U. A. Jacob, D.D., wrote: 'There is nothing in the New Testament which enjoins., ,or even mentions this ordinance " (confirmation). Dr. Edwards, late Dean of Bangor, ridicules the rite in the strongest terms. I find in the Communion Offer the words " the table," "Lord's table " " holy table," but altar is never named for the plain reason that the Reformers swept the thing itself away and substituted in place and word a table. Such men as Dr. Jayne retain the Popish term altar so as to make themselves sacrificing priests. I agree that churchmen, as per article six, ought to have a scriptural reason given them for both infant baptism and confirma- tion—Prove all things Andrew Willet, D.D., once preben- dary of Ely, wrote :—" The Bible is the chief judge, and ought so to be in all controversies; we may appeal from the Church to the Scriptures, not from the Scriptures to the Church" (or Prayer Book.) The Church is subject to the Scriptures ; the rule of faith is to the Scriptures not to the Church, the Church is not the chief judge of Scriptures, but itself is to be judged by the Scriptures. • ROBERT FOULKES. ' July 2, 1891.

div.head: THINGS TIF.A.RD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS TIF.A.RD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Mr. J. J. Brunner, M.P. for the Northwich Divi- sion, has just been elected president of the 'Sunday Society, and on Saturday he delivered his presiden- tial address in the Lady Brassey Museum, London. On the question of Sunday observance as well as on other subjects Mr. Brunner is broad and tolerant. The object of the Sunday Society, he said, was to maintain and enhance the value and importance of the English Sunday. A greater attendance at libra- ries and museums meant a leas drawing of beer, and people who went to libraries needed much less at- tention than people who went to public houses, so that in this view of the subject Mr. Brunner argued that the success of the Society meant a better ful- filment of the commandment enjoining a weekly day of rest. Mr. Brunner had seen Sunday in a good many parts of the Continent and of England and while none were perfect, the British Sunday of the slums, with its deadening vacuity, its gluttony, and its debauchery, was certainly one of the ugliest spots on the civilisation of the nineteenth century. To remedy this state of affairs, to make Sunday a brighter and more enjoyable day, is the aim and end of the Society.

No one can speak of the habits and wishes of the working classes with more authority than Mr. Brunner, and he testifies that a larger proportion attend public worship to-day than was ever the case before in our time, and he was told this was very marked in towns where libraries and museums are open on Sunday. They were, moreover, gentler in manners and in speech. A foreman or ganger whe freely employ ed oaths and coarse and abusive lan- guage had much less influence and smaller command over his men than the foreman who most nearly approached the standard of him termed "gentle- man," and workmen of to-day would strongly re- sent any approach to the standard of 30 years ago, when the foreman who kept a civil tongue in his head was the exception. No doubt the spread of education has had much to do with this change, and the Sunday Society wish to give the poor and ignorant on the day on which they have the most leisure, an opportunity of making the acquaintance of" our best and truest friends, the best authors and artists of all ages." With such a noble object in view, the Sunday society ought not to lack mem- bers and supporters.

In the course of his speech Mr. Brunner made an important reference to a subject which has co m- manded great attentions in several by-elections. Th e eight hours day, in his opinion, is still a dream not within measurable distance, nor within the range of practical politics.

The Runcorn Burial Board goes on the even tenour of its way undisturbed by the turmoil th at eccasionally besets the other local bodies. A rate- payers' meeting was held the other evening to elect three members of the Board, but no business coul d be transacted until Mr. Salkeld's assistant, Mr. W. Jones, had been uut tb the byeways and hedges and brought two in to form a quorum. The business is 1 so well conducted that the ratepayers feel they could not leave it in better hands, and the retiring mem- bers were unanimously re-elected—viz., Messrs. W. Whittaker, W. Mellor, and E. Imison.

The news that Mr. Thomas Snape the represen- tative of Widnes on the Lancashire bounty Council, has been selected to contest the Heywood division at the next election, had been received in Widnes with much pleasure. Mr. Snape is a Liberal of advanced views, and describes himself to his future constituents as a " Gladstonian of the Radical Wing." He is a recognised authority on educa- tional affairs, and occupies the responsible position of Chairman of the Technical Instruction Commit- tee of the County Council. H 6 is a member of the Financial Refcrm Association and of the Peace Society, and he has made a study of the financial position of the country. As a speaker lie is eloqu- ent, clear, and bright, occasionally pressing home his arguments by most apposite anecdotes and quo- tations. In religion Mr. Snape is a United Free Methodist, and his serviced are much valued as a "local preacher." Heywood will have a most worthy representative if he is elected.

Yesterday afternoon the Technical Education Corn- mittea of the Cheshire County Council held a meet- ing at Crewe,to consider the numerous applications made for grants. Mr. Philip Speakman is a member of this Committee: and being also a member of the Board of Commissioners, he would be able to press with due weight the claims of Runcorn. It is a pity no effort is made to capture Mr. Brunner's prof erred thousand.

The news of the tragical death of Superinten- dent Hollingworth was received in Runcorn where he had spent so many years of his life with regret and sadness. The best of men are not without their faults, and no one would wish to suggest that Supt. Hollingworth was a perfect man, but he was a smart and clever officer, and his genial disposition made him hosts of friends in every town in which he was stationed. He was followed to his last rest- ing place by the Chief Constable and the Borough Police of Stockport, six County Superintendents, and a large number of the County Constabulary. Numerous civilians, and representatives of various Masonic Lodges in Cheshire—a testimony to the re- spect and regard in which he was held despite the shafts hurled against him some months ago. He will be succeeded by Detective-Inspector Bretton.

div.head: BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.

. I was surprised last week, after my remarks the week previous anent the new church at Haydock, to find a letter signed by the whole of the wardens and sidesmen, to the effect that they were powerless to act in the matter. I suppose they mean by this, that they are unable to secure the formal opening of the building. This is rather stranae. news, espe- cially coming from such a quarter. 'Have they no influence with the vicar, and if not cannot they move independently? To my mind the new church is in a fair way to become a white elephant, and this is the more surprising when it is known that a great cry was raised some time ago for more room for the worshippers. At the present time the aver- age congregation numbers about 300. Wherefore then a new church.

. Gradually they are moving in the van of civilisa- tion:at Haydock. The Local Board authorities have decided to buy a water cart, in order to keep down any dust which might in very dry weather prove obstreperous. It appears in Haydock, that the roads get so fearfully dry, that the macadam stones break loose from their moorings and goin search of water, and two men are usually employed to arrest the re- calcitrant stones. Now, however, things are to be altered and water will be brought to the spot.

The sense of decency appears to be observed in Haydock, in a very minor degree. It appears the township is provided with a reservoir, in which the water used for domestic purposes is stored. In addition to a place of storage, it is used as a bath- ing depot, and also a place in which dogs are allowed to disport themselves. The bare idea of being compelled to drink water, in which several grimy colliers, and their. dogs, live washed them- selves, is sufficient to give " a " to the most ardent teetotaller. It is about time a stop was put to such disgraceful proceedings.
I was deeply sorry to hear of the death of Mrs.
. Emmett, as she was a lacizl, ivlinni-everybady turned with respect. She will be sadly missqd, and espetially will this be the cab among theterigious body with whom she was cot/heated.

I hear that something is at higt:beltik done to res- cuseitate the Liberal party in tlifbilivision. It is said that the reorganisation of ttn forces is being quietly carried on by some geneetnan sent down specially for the purpose. I hope this may be so, as it is out of the question to allow the Tories a walk over in such an important constituency.

div.head: ArOTHER CHARGED WITH MURDER
div.p: A ArOTHER CHARGED WITH MURDER
IN WALES. FEARFUL STORY OF CRUELTY.

On 'Thursday, at the Abergele Police Court, before Messrs. R. B. Hesketh and J. D. ,Miller, Catherine Roberts was charged with the wilful murder of her child, :Mary Ellen Roberts, eight years of age. From the evidence of several witnesses, neighbours of the prisoner, it appeared that the child had been subjected to the most cruel treatment by her mother, who knocked her to the ground frequently on the slightest provocation.—Dr. Wolstenholme stated that on the 30th of June he went to the prisoner's hoase, and saw there the body of the child. Under the chin was a large wound two inches in extent. He thought at first that someone had cut the child's throat. Nearly every portion of the body bore bruises and scars, some of which seemed to have been produced by blows with a stick or poker, or made with a hot iron. Maggie Williams, domestic servant at the Harp Inn. Abergele, also gave evidence as to the prisoner's cruel treatment of the deceased.—The case was adjourned at this stage to await the result of a post-mortem examina- tion and the verdict of a coroner's jury.

div.head: -•-- THE ASTON SENSATION.
div.p: -•-- THE ASTON SENSATION.
THE CHARGE OF ATTEMPTING TO POISON A HUSBAND.

At the Neston Police Court, yesterday afternoon, Mary Emily Scruby was charged on remand with attempting to poison her husband, Edward Roderick Scruby, a grocer and provision dealer, residing in Gladstone-road, and carrying on business in Bridge- st. The court was crowded, and the inhabitants of Neston manifested the greatest interest in the proceedings. Superintendent Hindley pro- secuted, and Mr. R. B. Moore defended. The prisoner last .week was allowed out on bail in her own recognisance of £2O, and two sure- ties of £lOO each. Mr. Moore, in making the application for bail, said that he would be able to show the entire innocence of his client when the case came before the court again. The evidence given previously was to the effect that the prose- cutor kept a lock-up shop. lie was in the habit of having oatmeal and water sent to him from home in the summer time. On the 12th of last month he received the drink as usual. When he drank a cup of it, and was about to take a second, he experi- enced a choking sensation in his throat, followed by severe pains in the stomach. information was given to the police, and the remainder of the fluid handed over to a sergeant. Evidence was given by Annie Constance Emilie Scruby, the daughter, eleven years of age, that she saw her mother mix the oatmeal and water in the same way. The prisoner was not arrested till the 13th, and when charged by Sergeant Jones, she made the following statement :—" It's him that ought to be locked up for kicking me; he has kicked a tooth out of my head, and kicked me on the back." Domestic differences, it is stated, have arisen bet- ween the parties recently, but previously they had ' lived happily together. Mr. Moore's statement that he would be able to prove the entire innocence of his client, together with another statement by Superintendent Hindley at the last sitting of the court to the effect that " there was something wrong somewhere," led to a great deal of specula- tion as to the line which the defence would take.

At the commencement of the case, Superinten- dent llindley complained to the Bench that a wit- ness had been assaulted last week. The Chairman said that to assault a witness was a very serious thing, and any one brought before the bench would be severely dealt with for such an offence. _ _

Sergeant Jones said he tasted the gruel, and it left a burning sensation. On gaining the house of prisoner he touud in the back kitchen a basin con- taining a small quantity of white liquid and on the wall in the side yard a jar containing liquid. lie took the articles to the public analyst. In reply to Mr. Moore, witness said that prosecu- tor on the 10th was alleged to have assaulted his wife. Ile did not know of his own knowledge that Mrs. Scruby was supplied by the police with a wbistle. - -

Mr. Bell, public analyst for Cheshire, said he had made an analysis of the articles received from the police. In the bottle of oatmeal and water he found four and a half grains of white precipitate, and halt a grain in the jug. The substance was a poison, being a compound of mercury, ammonia, and chlorine. White precipitate was not a violent poison.
Mrs. Grimwood, the hEroine of Manipur, had the honour of lunching with the Queen at Windsor Castle, on Wedncsday.

Mr. Parnell was born at Avondale, county Wick- low, in 1846. He is descended from an old English family that passed over from Congleton Cheshire, to Ireland, and many of his anoestors have played prominent parts in history. Thomas Parnell, the poet, was one of the family. Mr. Parnell's great grandfather, Sir John Parnell, held for many years the office of Chancellor of the Exchequer in the Irish Parliament, and resigned rather than vote for the Act of Union; and Sir Henry Parnell, Sir John's son, after many years service \in the House of Com- mons was raised to the peerage of Lord Congleton in 1841. Mr. Parnell's mother is the daughter of Admiral Charles Stewart, a celebrated American naval officer. Mr. Parnell was educated at various private schools in England, and at Magdalen College, Cambridge, from which it is said, "he was abruptly sent down' for knocking a man down, apparently in a fit of abstraction, and refusing to apologise." He was first returned to Parlia- ment for the county of Meath, after having fought an unsuccessful contest in the county of Dublin. The following extract from a "Pall Mall Gazette " " Extra," published in 1886, will be read with interest at the present time. We are told that "there has been no such sudden greatness thrust on a man in our time; what makes it the most remark- able is that the uncrowned King of Ireland, is only half an Irishman, not a great speaker, a Protestant and a landlord. Half Mr. Parnell's success is due to his wonderful gift of silence and his discreet reserve —a quality which serves him in good stead in his private as well as his public life. The veil has re- cently been lifted by a correspondent in the "Pall Mall Gazette," from the suburban retreat in which Mr. Parnell recuperates himself after the labours of the House. It is at Wonersh House, Eltham, Kent, although a letter would be better addressed to the Irish office,at least the clerks at the latter place will tell you so; but Mr. Parnell, by the way,adds to his gift of silence the not less valuable faculty of never answering letters." Mr. Parnell's methods' of " re- cuperation " at Eltham, Kent, have now become historical. They were recently set forth in some detail in the Divorce Court, with results in the poli- tical world that were rather startling. Mrs. Parnell is a sister of Sir Evelyn Wood, and has has much of the talent common to the gifted family ,which has contributed to the service of the State such a Chancellor as Lord Hatherley and such a general as Sir Evelyn Wood. Mrs. Parnell has been spoken of in these recentflays as if she had no claim to distinction other than that she has figured in a painful case with a prominent politician. But this is not so. She is a woman of winning manners, of strong will, of considerable abilities,and of great ambition. She is a keen politician, and was well equipped for playing the part of Egeria to a politi- cal leader. She lived with her son and daughters at Eltham a life of unconventional freedom,and her house presented just that mixture of domestic com- fort with intellectual cleverness which men im- mersed in the cares of public life so greatly enjoy. Of the life that Mr. Parnell led while staying in suburban retreat with Mrs. O'Shea, many accounts have been given. The friends met at many seaside resorts. They were together at Brighton and Hastings and :Eastbourne and Rye, and many other places. But it was at Wonersh Lodge, Eltham, and at Woodcroft, Motting- ham, tf:at Mrs. O'Shea generally received him. Ten years ago Mr. Parnell, the political ally of Mr, Biggar, was considered utterly impossible in Eng- lish society. The O'Sheas' was almost the only house in which he met members of his own class on those equal terms which are the salt of social life. The friendship was, it should be noted, as much political as domestic. Of Captain O'Shea's political services to Mr. Parnell everyone is well aware. But in Mrs. O'Shea also Mr. Parnell found an ally of no little political value. With her he discussed his schemes; to her he confided his hopes. In the anxious and troublous times through " which Mr. Parnell passed from 1880 to 1884, he was often ill as well as harassed. It was to Mrs. O'Shea that he repaired for counsel and for care; and it was in Mrs. O'Shea's house that he found solace and pro- tection—with what result everybody knows.
" OWD TAYPOT." A TOFFY MERCHANT FORTY YEAR SIN.

Owd Taypot browt a toffy stall To ey'ry Nyowton Fair; An' tho' he wur not quite a foo, No deawbt he'r rayt her quare. Eh ! if yo'd heerd him cry his goods, Yo never cud forget; Yo'll mebbe think aw'm stretchin. it, But aw con hear him yet! His fav'rite sung wur, "Here yo are, Rale Bassilony nuts; An' if eyt these yo'll escape Mitch trubble yer g—ts ! Aw've Awmskirk gingsgbread new baket I' Nyowton oons, tip=top; Ther aiquils yo con never buy I' anny other shop! Aw've traycle toffy, nicely rowlt I' pepper smooth an' white; An' sugarsticks will mak yore teeth To water for a bite! Heer's Eccles Cakes fro' Peasley cross, Aw corruns in an' eawt ; An' if yo'll ony try urn oncet, Yo'll never, lads, be beawt." But while he gammont th' owder folk, Th' owd lad cud allus feel Fer th' little childre thrutchin' reawnd, An' filled ther pockets weel. He cudn't stond ther hungry looks, That towd o' want an' need; He sed it gen him 't stummuck wartch, An' made his gizzert bleed. Poor Taypot ! sin' theau "cut thi stick," Sum forty year hes gone; But aw'm quite sure we cud ha sparet Weel molly a better mon !
Nyowton, 29th June, 1891.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRlDAY.—Confidence in cotton seems a fickle thing, and to-day is evapourating quite as fast as anybody could desire. The first estimate ef 10.000 bales is considered large enough to cover '! spot " transactions, and "futures" have been on the slide ever since the opening. Yarns are not in great request, manufacturers seem to have placed their pressing business last week, and now will only buy yarns as they sell cloth, which is a process that does not go on quite as freely as could be desired. In cloth rather more Indiainquiry is on the market, but somehow it does not get to business. Some China inquiry of a similar character is also reported. LATEST NEWS.
Mr. Spurgeon was better yesterday. CRICKET.
Players all out for 79 ;gentlemen won by innings and 54 runs. Rain stopped play at Tunbridge.
DEATH OF FIREMAN HENDERSON.
The Fireman named Henderson, who was injured at the fire at Messrs. Aitken and Wright's of Leith', di ed yesterday. This makes the second death.
BOILER EXPLOSION AT COVENTRY.
Yesterday morning a boiler exploded at Floyd and Floyd's Malleable Iron Works, Coventry, and five men and boys were injured—one seriously. The roof of the workshop was blown off.

div.head: WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING AT
div.p: WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING AT

• RUNCORN. The quarterly meeting of the Runcorn Wesleyan Circuit was held on Monday in Brunswick School. The proceedings commenced in the afternoon with the gathering of local preachers, and the usual business was transacted. Tea was provided and afterwards the general meeting was held under the presidency of the Rev. H. Burson, the super- intendent minister. The Stewards (Messrs. Simister and Pope) presented a financial state- ment which was considered highly satisfac- tory. The Chairman gave a statement showing the amount contributed to the various connexional funds during the year. On the proposition of the stewards a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the Revs. H. Burson, W. Kendrew and J. Judson. for their services during the three years they had been in the circuit. Several members of the Society spoke to this resolution in suitable terms. The thanks of the meeting were also presented to the local preachers for their long, continuous, and efficient services in the circuit. Mr. B. Kniveton introduced a discussion on the liquor traffic, and it was unanimously, resolved "That this meeting of representatives of the Wesleyan Methodist churches of this town and neighbourhood re- joices in the growing public opinion on the necessity for the restriction of the issuing of licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquors, and respectfully urges upon the magistrates the importance of exercising their powers in the interests of temperance and morality at the ensuing Brewster Sessions.' An influential deputation was ap- pointed to present the resolution to the magistrates, and urge the subject upon their consideration, and it was further resolved to invite the co-operation of the other Nonconformist churches of the town.

Mr. Davies, Lord Lieutenant of Anglesey, has given £l,OOO to form the nucleus of a special fund of £20,000 in connection with the Welsh Theological College at Bala. Twelve hundred workmen employed in the shipbuild ing yards at Greenock and Port Glasgow, struck work on Wednesday against a reduction of 5 per cent. in wages. President Harrison has issued a proclamation which provides for granting copyright in the United States to citizens or subjects of Great Britain, France, Belgium, and Switzerland.
PEN KETH.
TRIP TO LLANDUDNO,

The annual trip of the teachers, officers,and friends connected with the Wesleyan Sunday School took place on Saturday. It having been decided to visit Llandudno this year, arrangements were made with , Messrs. Crosfield, who were also going to Llandudno,' whereby the two trips were combined. The Penketh party, numbering 48, left Bank Quay Station, at 7 a.m., and after a quick and pleasant journey, Llan- dudno was reached about 9 15. Upon arrival the spirits of the patty, were somewhat damped, as it was found that the rain, which commenced falling shortly after leaving Chester, was still descending. However, by the time the hotel, where breakfast was provided, was reached,"the rain had ceased, and the weather during the remainder of the day was everything that could be desired. After breakfast, the trippers set out to see the 'sights• in and around Llandudno. Most of the party drove round the Great Orme's Head. The Little Orme, Conway Castle, and other places of interest were also visited, whilst a number of the pleasure-seekers climbed to the top of the Great Orme, from whence a magnifi- cent view was obtained. At half-past three all the , party meet for tea, which, after the day's exertions, ' was much enjoyed. After tea, the time was spent in visiting and viewing the shops in the town, and at 6.45 the excursionists met on the station. There It was found that the train, which was announced to start at 7 p.m., would not start till 7.30. Shortly before 7.30, however, a start was effected, and War- rington was reached about,lo.ls p.m.
WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, yesterday morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. W. Long, Heaton, Aukland, Dobson, John Houghton, W. Houghton, Kilshall, Smith, Humph- reys, Jolley, Swinton; S. Sutton (clerk), Dr. Seph- ton (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (inspector). DRAINAGE AT BITRTONWOOD.—A letter was read from the solicitors of the Collins Green Colliery Co., Limited, with respect to new sewers being required in the town- ship of Burtonwood. The Authority was asked to take steps for the provision of Avers for the houses there.— In the course of some discussion on this subject, Dr. Sephton said it was the intention of the Colliery Co. tap make a model place at Burtonwood. They were going to supply the electric light, and also put up a water tower for the supply of water.—lt was decided to refer the matter to Mr. Owen, to consider the feasibility of carrying out a drainage scheme. THE NEW RAILWAY.—A plan of the proposid new Lancashire,Derbyshire and East Coast Railway was sub- mitted to the Authority, and, on the motion of Mr. Jolley, seconded by Mr. Heaton. a resolution was passed unanimously approving of the Bill before Parliament for power to construct the railway. THE DEATH RATE.—Dr. Sepliton reported that the death-rate in the Authority's district for the past year was 22.1,as compared with 19.1 in the last three months, and 16.2 in the corresponding period of last year. The doctor reported that influenza was gradually but slowly passing away. arrim RECENT BOROUGH Ex.rmistox.—TheClerk reported that he had come to terms with the Town Clerk with reference to the amount to be paid for the sewers taken over by the Corporation under the Borough Extension Act. The net amount to be paid by the Corporation was £1,062. A resolution was passed authorising the Clerk to approach the Local Government Board and the Public Works Loan Board with a view to the redemption of the loan' and to place the balance to the credit of the dis- trict. This was the principal business.

div.head: WEDDING GIFTS AT WINDSOR,
div.p: WEDDING GIFTS AT WINDSOR,

Silver wedding gifts to Prince and Princess Christian. and wedding presents to their daughters were presented in the Guildhall, Windsor, yesterday afternoon. Prince Christian, addressing the citizens as friends and neigh- bours, expressed his warm thanks for the kindness always shown to him and his family by the people of Windsor.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE'S HEALTH.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S HEALTH.

It is announced that since Mr. Gladstone' arrival at Mr. Colman's residence, near Lowestoft, his health has undergone a decided improvement, and that he is now almost as well as he was before his attack of influenza. The Corporation of Newcastle-on-Tyne has resolved to confer the freedom of the city on Mr. Gladstone on the occasion of the visit of the National Liberal Federation in October.
Mr. Gladstone passed an excellent night, and is rapidly gaining strength.
THE BETTWS-Y-COED OUTRAGE.
STATEMENT BY MRS. DUNCAN.

The police have obtained from Mrs. Duncan a state- ment relative to the circumstances under which her hus- band murderously assaulted her on the evening of the 12th Hay, but will give no information as to its nature. The statement has been sent up to the Treasury for examination and further instructions. A late telegram says the depositions of Mrs. Duncan were taken yesterday. Shesays she has no recollection of her husbands attack upon her. THE LABOUR COMMISSION.

Mr. Falvy, of the London Labourers' Protection League, giving evidence on Thursday, before the Labour Commission, urged that employers should be held crim- inally responsible for defects in machinery which had been once pointed out. Witness also accused the Com- mission of want of attention. _ . _

Yesterday, James Donovan, of the Amalgamated Stevedores' Society, described the Shipping Federation as a body formed to break up the men's union. Sir John Gorst objected to the manner in which Mr. _Jesse Col- lings examined the witness, and a sharp altercation took place between the honourable members. The witness ad- vocated the municipalization of the docks, technical education and a system of State pensions—the married man with wife and family getting 30s. per week, the single men 20s. and women 15s.

div.head: CASE OF MRS. CATHCART.
div.p: THE CASE OF MRS. CATHCART.

Yesterday, Mr. Bulwer, Q.C., a Commissioner in Lunacy, and a special jury, resumed the inquiry in London, respecting the alleged lunacy of Mrs. Cathcart. Mr. Cathcart said that he proposed marriage to his wife in May, 1884, and was definitely accepted at the begin- ning of June. He entered into a covenant to tecure £5OO a year to his wife when he should succeed to his estate. His illness at Pitcarnie was caused by worry, following a chill. He occupied a separate bedroom because he thought he might sleep better. He was not suffering from the disease mentioned, and the statement that he committed adultery with Nellie Wilson was utterly un- founded. After his wife left him,he wrote affectionately asking her to return. It was untrue that he had stayed with Miss Edith Unwin as his mistress, or had tried to get his wife into an asylum. Mr. Cathcart was then cross-examined by Sir Charles Russell.—The case was adjourned till Monday.
DESTRUCTIVE VATER-SPOUT.-12 LIVES LOST.

A Vienna telegram says serious havoc has been caused by a waterspout that passed over several places near Murau in Styria, on Thursday. Two villages are said to have been almost entirely destroyed, and twelve per- sons to have lost their lives. TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN AMERICA.
PASSENGERS BURNED TO DEATH.
GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

CLEVELAND, FRIDAY.—A despatch has been received here stating that an east-bound train on the Erie Railway was run into by a freight train at Ravenna at three o'clock this morning. Two, sleeping cars and a day car- riage became ignited, and were entirely destroyed. it

is added that nineteen bodies have up to the present been removed from the wreckage. NEW YORK FRIDAY.—A terrible railway accident occur- red at three o'clock this morning on the Erie railroad. An eastern bound passenger train, well laden with travel lers, by some means at present unexplAined, came into collision with a heavy freight train at Ravenna, Ohio. The leading cars and waggons in both trains were completely wrecked. To add to the horrors of the scene, a fire broke out instantly among the wreckage, and the sufferings of the poor victims jammed among the debris and unable to I extricate themselves as the flames grew nearer and nearer to them were agonising to behold. The full ex- tent of the catastrophe is not yet known, but nineteen bodies have.already been taken from the wreckage. Of these the majority were so mutilated or charred by fire as to be quite unrecognisable. It is almost certain that other bodies remain beneath the burning wreckage, as several passengers have yet to be accounted for. Scarcely a single passenger escaped without hurt of some sort, and no fewer than 38 sustained serious in- juries. Urgent appeals have been made to adjoining towns for medical assistance, and already a special train conveying a number of physicians and surgeons has started from Cleveland for the scene of the disaster.
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House of Lords met at ten o'clock, when the Royal assent was given by commission to the Consolidated Fund, the Customs and Inland Revenue, the Pollen Fisheries (Ireland), the Public Accounts and Charges, and to about 50 provisional orders and private bills. The lArd Commissioners were the Lord Chancellor, the Duke of Portland, and the Earl of Limerick. The House adjourned at half-past ten. AFTERNOON SITTING.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. MISCELLANEOUS .—The Earl of Delawar moved for the repert of the Board of Trade relative to the recent acci- dent on board the City of Richmond. Lord BALFOUR re- plied that there was DO official report, but all the infor- mation in the hands of the Government would be laid on the table. The Mortmain and Charitable Uses Bill passed through Committee, and the Schools for Science and Art Bill passed through Committee. 'I he Fisheries Bill was read a third time, and the House adjourned at 5-40.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

AN EARLY SirriNG.—The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past ten o'clock, when the only other mem- ber present was Mr. McClure. The early hour of the sitting was rendered necessary in order to receive the Royalassent to a number of Acts. The sitting was resumed at three o'clock: PRIVATE BUSINESS.—The Lords amendments to the Manchester. Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway (Vari- ous Powers) Bill and the Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway Bill were agreed to. The Imperial Insurance, Plymouth, Devonport, and South Western Junction Railway, Neath Harbour, and Bourne- mouth East Cemetery Bills were read a third time. "ONLY Two CASES."—Sir M. HICKS-BEACH, in answer to Mr. Cobb, said there had been only two cases under which provisional orders had been made for the compul- sory acquirement of land under the Allotment Act, 1887. THE ALDERSHOT CASE.—The Home Secretary in- foribed the House that a sworn inquiry would be made into conduct of the Aldershot police in arresting Miss IMillwood,and swearing that she was a known prostitute.

TERRIBLE DEATH OF A JOURNALIST
SWALLOWED BY VESU V lUS.

NAPLES, THURSDAY Nrciirr.—On Monday night a young Brazilian journalist, Dr. Silva Jardim. who had gone up Vesuvius with a friend and one guide, met with a horrible death. He and his companions were all standing.on the edge of the central crater, when they were enveloped in a cloud of smoke. When it cleared away Dr. Jardim had disap- peared. His friend, who was also on the point of falling, was dragged back by the guide and saved.
The-deceased-Was much -esteem-ed in his native city Rio Janeiro. His wife and children he had left in Paris.
SIR HORATIO LLOYD AND COSTS.

The "Daily News" says :—The mind of the Chairman of the Cheshire Court of Sessions is per- turbed, and not without reason, on the subject of the costs which accompany the fines inflicted for petty offences. Tiiere are, he observes, a great many persons now in prison for no other reason than their inability to pay these demands, and he is desirous of finding some means of reducing their number. Sometimes magistrates knowing that the costs will be heavy, reduce the fines, from a humane desire not to bear too hardly on a prisoner; but this, as Sir Horatio Lloyd remarks, is not quite a regular practice. The Summary Jurisdic- tion Act provides that no costs shall be inflicted where the fine is not more than five shillings. From the fact, however, that the Secretary of State has addressed a letter to all magistrates' clerks drawing attention to this clause it may be inferred that it is sometimes overlooked. What is'wanted is uniformity of practice and a reasonable scale.

Education Bill.—Sir R. TEMPLE moved to leave out Words empowering the Education Depot to supply accommoda- tion in any district without fees upon representations that the present accommodation is insufficient. He thought Voluntary Schools would not be able to keep their heads above water, if the section was adopted in the ' present form.—Sir W. HENRY DYKE defended the section. After further discussion, Mr. W. H. &writ in opposing the amendment, said he was sure that, under the Bill, the varied character of English schools would be main- tained. The amendment would destroy the Bill Mr. IVIOWBRAY contended that, under the Bill, all voluntary schools in the country would be placed at the mercy of a hostile minority.—Mr. DR lastig saw no objection to the proposal that Board Schools should be establisfted where voluntary schods could not do the work. On a division that subsection was retained by 169 to 38. Mr. SUM- MERS moved to omit the words the expiration of one year," so that the representation might be made imme- diately after the commencement of the act.—Sir W. HART DYER opposed the amendment. The words were inserted in the clause for the purpose of giving the voluntary schools time to prepare for the exigencies of the act.—Mr. Murroßm.s. had hope that the Government would at least have met the advocates of the amend- ment half-way and to substitute six months for one year. Aftey a short discussion the amendment was rejected by(l66 to 95.

TITE LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR THE HEY WOOD DIVISION. On Thursday evening, a meeting of the Execu- tive of the Liberal Council far the Heywood Divi- -sion of Lancashire, was held at Bury, to receive the report of the sub-committee appointed to consider the selection of a candidate. Mr. Thomas Snape, of Widnes and Liverpool, was recommended, and he was present and addressed the executive., At the close of his address, it was unanimously re- solved to recommend that Mr. Snape he the candi- date for the division at the next election.
